column20: Two imputation approaches were used to fill missing country–year data: Linear interpolation/extrapolation connects existing data points within a country. Machine learning via LASSO regression predicts missing test scores using 501 World Bank indicators (economic, demographic, and educational). The two methods produced highly correlated estimates (r=0.967), confirming consistency.
column21: Results showed high consistency between the two imputation methods (r=0.967) and strong predictive performance (R²=0.91, RMSE?17.5). Test scores for 15-year-olds were transformed into annual educational-quality indicators for the 15–19 age cohort and into educational-quality indices for the working-age population (15–64). The analyses revealed a positive correlation between educational quality and average years of schooling (r=0.67), with countries such as Japan, South Korea, and Singapore exhibiting both high learning quality and extended schooling duration.
column22: This study introduces a comprehensive cross-national dataset enabling global comparisons of educational quality from 1970 to 2023. By harmonizing PISA, TIMSS, and IEA data, it supports analysis of long-term educational trends. However, differences in test design and population coverage, the imputation of nearly half of country–year observations, and reliance on World Bank indicators for LASSO regression may introduce uncertainty and simplify complex educational dynamics. The dataset includes harmonized test scores for 15-year-olds, annual quality indicators for ages 15–19, and educational quality indices for the working-age population (15–64).

column25: Background: PISA 2022 results, U.S. students earned the lowest math scores in two decades. column21: Language-related themes were more prevalent in Singapore’s mathematics curriculum than in Hong Kong’s. column22: The study examined how language and mathematics skills relate within Singapore and Hong Kong curricula using ANN and ANFIS models. These findings suggest that while curriculum design influences the link between language and math, broader factors—such as teaching quality, socio-economic conditions, and student motivation—have greater impact. column20: The study used analytical proofs and a simulation study manipulating three conditions: item difficulty, number of items (J), and missing data. column21: Increasing predictors (P) causes significant bias when measurement precision is low: population means become negative, variances inflate, and percentiles distort outward. This bias is non-linear and disproportionately affects low-proficiency groups. Notably, 2PL models are robust with only 4–6 items, whereas 3PL models require much more data to avoid bias due to the "guessing" parameter.
column22: Instabilities in LSAs stem from the non-linearity of the IRT model interacting with small sample-to-predictor ratios. Valid group-level inference depends on ensuring "moderate measurement precision" for all students. Providing every student with at least 4–6 2PL items makes the model robust enough to handle hundreds of background variables effectively.
column23: Findings apply strictly to "boundary conditions" with low item counts and small sample-to-predictor ratios. In large datasets or assessments with many items (>10) per scale, bias approaches zero. The study also assumes homoscedasticity (constant residual variance), which may not reflect more complex real-world data
column24: Suggested refinements include testing regularization (LASSO, Ridge) instead of PCA for high-dimensional data, applying Bayesian priors to stabilize small-sample subgroups, and integrating process data (e.g., response times) as indicators to increase precision without lengthening tests.
column25: This paper is a significant contribution to the field of computational psychometrics as it clarifies a long-standing debate. It refutes the previous belief that PV-based estimators are perfectly consistent with plug-in estimators under current operational procedures (like those in NAEP), showing instead that sampled regression parameters introduce a specific positive bias. It serves as a technical manual for test developers to optimize the balance between assessment length and the scope of variables used for reporting.

Identified items were grouped into composite variables, validated through reliability and CFA checks, or PCA when model fit was poor. column20: Reading self-concept was measured with a reliable three-item scale. From 1,482 available variables, Elastic Net (ENET) was applied separately at the student, teacher, and school levels to select the most influential predictors. An expert panel then reviewed these variables, and composite measures were created and validated through CFA or PCA. Variables with over 20% missingness were removed, and remaining missing data were imputed using PMM for ENET and two-level FCS for multilevel models. Teacher variables were aggregated to the school level, and two-level multilevel modeling with sampling weights and centering was used to examine predictors of reading self-concept for the full sample and separately for emergent bilinguals and native English speakers.
column21: ENET and multilevel analyses showed that student-level factors were the strongest predictors of reading self-concept. column22: Reading habits, perceived ICT competence, work mastery, and teacher understanding are the strongest positive predictors of adolescents’ reading self-concept, while excessive ICT use, socioeconomic disadvantage, and negative emotions negatively influence it. column21: The topic modeling analysis identified six major themes in the LSA process-data literature: response time models, general response-time research, aberrant test-taking behaviors, action sequence analyses, complex problem solving, and digital writing. Research on aberrant behaviors focused on detecting disengagement or guessing, while action-sequence and CPS studies used clickstream patterns to classify strategies, predict performance, and identify latent subgroups. Digital writing studies investigated typing behaviors and process features, consistently showing that planning, fluency, and editing behaviors meaningfully relate to writing performance.
column22: Most studies concentrate on response-time analyses and methodological model development, while areas like reading- and math-specific process data remain comparatively underexplored. Overall, the review points to promising directions for future research, including expanding process-data types, strengthening theoretical foundations, and exploring underexamined domains.

column20: The study followed the PRISMA framework and used the PICO strategy to systematically identify research applying AI models to evaluate educational performance in basic education. Searches were conducted across major scholarly databases (ERIC, IEEE, Scopus, ScienceDirect, and Web of Science) using predefined keywords related to education and AI. After removing duplicates and screening titles, abstracts, and full texts based on strict inclusion–exclusion criteria, 70 eligible articles published between 2000 and 2021 were selected. All articles were then coded for population, methods, educational level, data source, and AI techniques to synthesize patterns in how AI has been used in educational performance research.
column21: The review identified 70 studies using AI models to evaluate educational performance, showing a sharp increase in publications especially after 2015 with 2020 being the most productive year. Most studies used elementary school data, relied heavily on publicly available datasets (particularly from Portugal, Türkiye, and Brazil), and focused either on comparing AI models or predicting student performance. Classification methods, neural networks, decision trees, SVMs, and regression models were the most common techniques, with R, Weka, and Python as the primary analysis tools. Overall, the findings show growing interest in applying AI to education, but with limited adoption in developing regions and minimal translation of results into practical policy actions.
column22: Growing interest using AI to analyze educational performance, yet this growth is uneven, with limited from developing regions such as Latin America, Africa, and Asia. Although AI methods offer powerful capabilities for handling large datasets and uncovering hidden patterns, their adoption in education is hindered by interpretability challenges and the “black-box” nature of many models. Also AI can support both macro-level policy analysis and micro-level instructional decision-making, but most research still focuses on technical model comparisons rather than practical educational insights. Integrating SHAP, LIME and improving data quality are essential for translating AI findings into actionable educational policies.
column23: The review is limited by the small number of eligible studies, despite an initially large pool of search results, reflecting the scarcity of AI-based educational performance research that meets rigorous criteria. Geographic coverage is uneven, with no studies from Oceania and very few from developing regions such as Latin America, Africa, and parts of Asia, which restricts the generalizability of the findings. Additionally, many studies rely on complex “black-box” AI models whose limited interpretability makes practical policy application challenging.
column24: Future studies should incorporate longitudinal datasets and apply interpretable AI techniques (LIME, SHAP) to overcome the “black-box’’ barrier and better track changes in educational performance over time. Researchers are encouraged to integrate both traditional large-scale surveys and emerging data from educational technologies to generate richer, more actionable evidence for policy-making. Expanding analyses to underrepresented regions will be essential to developing globally relevant insights and supporting more equitable educational improvements.
column25: An important consideration regarding the use of AI models in education is the quality of the data. Insufficient or incomplete data, including the presence of null values, can lead to inaccurate and unreliable patterns. Artificial Intelligence models require large amounts of high-quality data in order to generate accurate and meaningful insights. However given the limited availability of data at the level of individual public schools, it may be necessary to broaden the scope of analysis to include data from larger geographic areas, such as municipalities or states.
column26: This can help ensure that the data used for AI analysis is sufficiently robust and representative of the education system as a whole. column20: The study employed two complementary analytical methods: Process Mining (PM) and Latent Profile Analysis (LPA). PM was used to extract and visualize students’ step-by-step actions from log files, generating process models that reveal common patterns, strategies, and deviations during Task 1. LPA was then applied to Task 2 to identify latent student groups based on exploration behavior, strategy use, response time, and accuracy, followed by MANOVA to examine how inquiry-based teaching practices differed across the identified profiles.
column21: Varied levels of inquiry performance across Task 1 and Task 2, with clear differences in exploration behavior, strategy use, and response accuracy. In Task 2, latent profile analysis identified three distinct groups (strategic, emergent, and disengaged) each characterized by different levels of exploration, strategy use, and task success. Students in the strategic profile showed the strongest performance and were more frequently exposed to inquiry-based classroom practices, particularly class debates, which uniquely differentiated all three profiles.
column22: Students experienced difficulties in univariable and multivariable reasoning, as well as in coordinating theory with evidence, despite being able to generate data through simulations. Moreover, exposure to certain inquiry-based practices (classroom debates) was associated with higher inquiry performance, highlighting the importance of active engagement in inquiry-oriented learning environments.
column23: The analysis revealed three profiles—strategic, emergent, and disengaged—differing in exploration levels, strategy use, and task success. column20: The study used PISA 2018 science log data, focusing on two science clusters that contained 38 items with rich process data. column21: Key process data indicators (user missingness and time to last visit) were strongly associated with test-taking motivation and academic performance. column22: Process data can validly capture test-taking motivation, with behavioral effort emerging as a robust and meaningful indicator beyond traditional self-report and response-time measures. In the area of mathematics education, has seen a steady increase of studies taking log data into account to advance our understanding of student cognitive and behavioral processes. Some of this work has taken place in the context of online learning or tutoring environments (Kerr & Chung, 2012; Martin et al., 2015; Gobert et al., 2015; Derr et al., 2018; Hrastinski et al., 2021; Olsher et al., 2023), whereas others have analyzed log data coming from collaborative, formative or summative assessment (Salles et al., 2020; Jiang et al., 2021; Mohan et al., 2020; Faber et al., 2017; Reis Costa et al., 2021; Jiang et al., 2023; Araneda et al., 2022). column21: The review identified remarkably few K-12 studies that addressed ethical, privacy, and regulatory issues in the use of process data, with only three studies meeting the criteria despite the growing prevalence of digital assessment. When the scope was broadened to higher education and general educational contexts, 22 studies were included, yet ethical considerations remained limited, often appearing only as brief mentions rather than integrated components of research design. Across studies, privacy and transparency received slightly more attention, while core issues such as responsibility, data stewardship, fairness, and validity were largely absent. Overall, the findings reveal substantial gaps in how ethical and regulatory dimensions are incorporated into process-data-based assessment research, especially in empirical and assessment studies.
column22: While the use of process data in digital assessments is rapidly expanding, ethical, privacy, and regulatory considerations remain significantly under-addressed, especially in K-12 contexts. Most studies focus heavily on technical analysis of log data, whereas issues such as validity, fairness, informed consent, data stewardship, and minimising potential harm receive limited and inconsistent attention. Existing assessment standards have not kept pace with the methodological developments surrounding process data, highlighting the need for a dedicated ethical framework tailored to educational assessment. The review concludes by calling for updated standards and more empirical research that explicitly integrates ethical safeguards into the design and use of process data in assessment.
column23: The review is limited by the timing of its data collection, which ended just before the introduction of GDPR in 2018, capturing practices that may have since changed. column27: when they make their first answer-related event. It denotes the duration while students understand instructions and conceptually plan their actions, before making any. Execution time (ET) is defined as the time difference between students’ first and last answer-related events. It measures the duration while students execute their planned actions. Mean execution time per (MET) is measured as ET divided by the number of answer related events.3 ET reflects total efforts of students casted to construct their answers, including setting up answers and revising or (possibly) reviewing their choices, whereas MET reflects average effort over total events. Controlling for answer-related events, MET indicates the efficiency of action execution.

The n-gram approach offers several benefits. Furthermore, Intraclass Correlation Coefficient was lower in the listwise deletion model (0.35) compared to the imputed model (0.44), proving that deleting missing cases distorts the hierarchical variance.
column22: While listwise deletion remains a "de facto" accepted approach in many current publications, it is mathematically one of the worst methods for handling missingness in large-scale assessments as it ignores uncertainty and biases results. Multiple imputation is a superior strategy because it accounts for both within-imputation and between-imputation variance through Rubin’s Rules. The R/Blimp workflow provides a replicable way to generate efficient standard errors while respecting nested data structures.
column23: The current workflow is computationally demanding, requiring nearly 50 minutes for 200 models without parallelization. column25: A key contribution is the "m × PV" rule, which mandates that a full set of imputations must be performed for every plausible value provided in the dataset. column21: Female students outperform male students in creative thinking (Est. = -0.277) and reading (Est. = -0.294) consistently across countries; math shows no substantial gender difference (Est. = 0.028). column22: Creative thinking performance reflects a mix of cognitive, motivational, and contextual factors rather than "pure" creative potential. The near-identical predictor patterns across facets provide little support for their theoretical distinction, questioning whether separate facet sub-scores are useful. Score dependence on booklet composition raises comparability concerns; the authors recommend using the full 32-item set where possible. The study shows the value of ML and XAI for construct validation.
column23: No standalone limitations section; the analysis addresses only convergent validity, not factorial validity, reliability, or dimensionality; findings are correlational, not causal.
column24: Disentangle creative thinking from general-ability and engagement confounds; use process data to study facets from a psychometric or cognitive-process angle; conduct cross-cultural and qualitative research to clarify what the assessment actually captures.
column25: Part of a special issue on PISA's Creative Thinking assessment; analyzes construct validity at the item level using ML+XAI, critiquing OECD's practice of aggregating scores across facets and domains; notably uses ALE plots over PDPs to avoid implausible predictor combinations.

column2: Hui Chen, Hongji Deng, Hao Yu, Yan Dong, and Huazhen Wang
column4: Interpretable Machine Learning Reveals Key Determinants of Creative Thinking Among East Asian Students: Evidence From PISA 2022
column8: PISA 2022; creative thinking; factors influencing creative thinking; interpretable machine learning; SHAP method
column9: 5 East Asian economies: Hong Kong (China), Macau (China), Chinese Taipei, South Korea, Singapore
column11: Student-level creative thinking scores (WLE, standardized) plus 30 candidate predictors across five dimensions: basic demographics, academic performance, socio-emotional characteristics, attitudes toward creative thinking, and digital technology use/self- efficacy, plus family and school environment indicators
column12: 29,208 students (48.62% female) Hong Kong (5,907), South Korea (6,454), Macau (4,384), Singapore (6,606), Chinese Taipei (5,857)
column13: Five predictive models compared: Elastic Net Regression, SVR, RF Regression, XGBoost, and LightGBM (selected as best model); SHAP; Leave-One-Group-Out Cross-Validation; KNN imputation; nested resampling (80/20 train/test split repeated 100 times)
column15: Creative thinking
column16: 30 predictors including academic performance, ESCS, GENDER, digital self-efficacy, expected educational attainment, empathy, attitude toward creative thinking, creative family climate, plus other socio-emotional, digital use, and family/school environment indicators
column17: To use interpretable machine learning (LightGBM + SHAP) to identify the key determinants of creative thinking among East Asian secondary students, characterize the directionality/ heterogeneity (including non-linear/ threshold effects) of these relationships, and uncover feature interactions shaping creative thinking in this high-achieving, examination-oriented cultural contextç
column18:
1. What are the key determinants of creative thinking among East Asian middle school students, and what is their relative importance?
2. How do the relationships between these key factors and creative thinking vary in terms of directionality and heterogeneity? 
3. How do interactions between these critical factors shape creative thinking in the East Asian context?
column19: Categorical variables label-encoded, continuous variables Z-score standardized; missing values imputed via KNN, fit only on training data within each split to prevent leakage; dataset randomly split 80/20 (train/test) and repeated 100 times with unique random seeds for robustness; hyperparameters tuned per model; LOGO-CV conducted as an additional robustness check to test whether model performance depended on economy specific characteristics.
column20: Compared 5 regression models (ENR, SVR, RFR, XGBoost, LightGBM) via cross-validated R^2; LightGBM performed best (R^2=0.63) and was selected for SHAP-based interpretability analysis, including global feature importance, dependence plots for directionality, and interaction-effect analysis.
column21: LightGBM had the highest accuracy (R^2=0.63) among the 5 models. Top predictors were reading, science, and math performance, ESCS, and gender. Reading and science showed near-linear positive links to creative thinking; ESCS, math, empathy, and digital self-efficacy showed threshold effects (best within an optimal range); creative family climate and expected education level showed negative links. The strongest interactions were reading x ESCS, science x gender, and science x ESCS.
column22: While some predictors match prior PISA findings, their nonlinear and interactive roles offer a more refined basis for designing creativity interventions than simple linear analysis. The reversed ESCS-achievement pattern and gender by science interaction suggest creativity support should be tailored by student subgroup, not applied uniformly. A robustness check showed LightGBM's advantage was partly inflated by economy-specific patterns, so its edge shouldn't be over-interpreted.
column23: No comparative data from other cultural regions limits generalizability beyond East Asia; interaction effects don't establish causality; the robustness check confirmed LightGBM's superiority was partly inflated by economy-specific sensitivity, so findings may not generalize beyond similar East Asian systems.
column24: Use the global PISA database to test how broader cultural values moderate creative thinking; conduct longitudinal/ experimental studies (randomized trials with differentiated creativity support) to test the causal mechanisms behind the interaction effects.
column25: One of the first applications of interpretable ML (LightGBM + SHAP) to PISA 2022's new Creative Thinking domain in East Asia; notable for using a robustness check that honestly qualifies rather than inflates its headline finding.

column2: Fernando Martínez-Abad, Adriana Gamazo, and María-José Rodríguez-Conde
column4: Educational Data Mining: Identification of Factors Associated With School Effectiveness in PISA Assessment
column8: School Effectiveness; Large-scale assessments; Educational Data Mining; Academic Achievement; Hierarchical Linear Modeling
column11: School- and student-level data from PISA 2015 covering performance in reading, mathematics, and science, along with context questionnaire scales on input and process variables administered to principals, teachers, and students.
column12: 32,330 students and 976 schools; reduced to 896 schools and 31,236 students. Phase 2: 239 schools and 8,347 students
column13: Hierarchical Linear Modeling / multilevel models (empirical Bayes estimation of school-level residuals), DTs with 10-fold stratified cross-validation
column14: HLM 7 (multilevel modeling); Weka 3.8.1, algorithm J48/C4.5 (decision tree construction)
column15: Phase 1: student performance in mathematics, reading, and science (used to compute school-level residuals). Phase 2: school effectiveness classification (dichotomous: high- vs. low-effectiveness, based on Phase 1 residuals).
column16: Input variables: gender, birth month, grade, ESCS index, immigrant status, grade repetition, number of school changes, mother tongue; school size, classroom size, resource/staff shortages, school ownership, student/teacher ratio, average ESCS, repeater rate, immigrant rate, proportion of girls. Process variables: 59 school- and aggregated student-level variables.
column17: To propose and test an innovative two-phase methodology combining multilevel modeling and educational data mining (decision trees) to identify process-level factors associated with school effectiveness in secondary education, using PISA 2015 Spanish data.
column18:
1. Identify high- and low-effectiveness schools using multilevel models based on input variables.
2. Identify process factors most predictive of school effectiveness using decision trees, and evaluate the suitability of decision trees for large-scale assessment data.
column19: Multilevel models run with 10 PVs and sample weights, robust estimators, missing data handled via low-percentage exclusion and regression imputation; schools classified as high-effectiveness or low-effectiveness; decision tree phase used student-level variables aggregated to school level, weighted by sample weights, tree size capped at 30 branches/minimum 15 instances per node, validated via 10-fold stratified cross-validation and tested for stability across 10 sub-samples.
column20: Phase 1: Multilevel (hierarchical linear) modeling to calculate school residuals and classify schools by effectiveness. Phase 2: C4.5/J48 decision tree classification using process variables as predictors and effectiveness classification as the target, evaluated via training-set fit and cross-validation (TP rate, precision, ROC-AUC, kappa, RRSE)
column21: ICC exceeded 10% in all 3 models, confirming sufficient school-level variance. Decision tree (25 branches, 13 leaves, 11 predictors) showed high fit, outperforming prior EDM studies. Low effectiveness linked to: excessive extracurricular lessons, excessive ICT use (though autonomous use was positive), non-optimal reading time, excessive principal autonomy, and extreme student attitudes toward cooperation/environmental optimism. High-effectiveness schools showed moderate, non-extreme values overall.
column22: The two-phase methodology outperformed prior EDM studies and avoided bias from using gross performance as outcome. Results align with prior literature on extracurricular lessons, ICT, and instructional time, but with more precise thresholds; supports an inverse relationship between principal autonomy and effectiveness. Confirms decision trees as a useful complement to multilevel modeling.
column23: Cross-sectional design precludes causal inference; inconsistency across PISA cycles limits replicability; Spanish-only sample limits generalizability; selecting only outlier schools excluded ~70% of the sample; use of aggregated student data at school level raises interpretive concerns.
column24: Replicate in other regions; address aggregation biases; conduct longitudinal studies; explore other techniques such as random forest.
column25: Proposes a novel two-phase method (multilevel modeling + decision trees) within the Effective Schools Movement tradition, using the CIPO framework; strong methodological focus with implications for policy at macro, meso, and micro levels.

column2: Li Zhu, Hyesun You, Minju Hong, and Zhenhan Fang
column4: Predictive Insights Into U.S. Students' Mathematics Performance on PISA 2022 Using Ensemble Tree-Based Machine Learning Models
column8: PISA 2022; mathematics performance; predictor selection; tree-based ML models; ALE plots
column11: Student- and school-level data on mathematics performance and 143 derived predictor variables spanning student background, affective variables, learning opportunities, and school- level factors.
column13: Three ensemble tree-based ML models: Random Forest (RF), XGBoost, and LightGBM; Accumulated Local Effects (ALE) plots; Wilcoxon signed-rank test
column15: Students' mathematics performance (PISA 2022 plausible values)
column16: 143 derived variables from student and school questionnaires; ML-selected top predictors includedmath self-efficacy, ESCS, familiarity with math concepts, expected occupational status, family support for self-directed learning, paid work, feelings about learning at home, ICT resources at home, math anxiety, exercise/sports practice
column17: To use ensemble tree-based ML models (RF, XGBoost, LightGBM) as an innovative, more objective alternative to literature-review-based predictor selection for identifying the factors most strongly associated with U.S. students' PISA 2022 math performance, interpret these predictors via ALE plots, and directly compare ML-selected vs. literature-review selected predictors.
column18:
1. What are the most influential predictors associated with students' math performance using ML models? 
2. How can we interpret students' math performance using the predictors obtained from the ML model? 
3. How do the predictors obtained by ML differ from those in the PISA literature?
column19: 143 derived variables constructed from student/school questionnaires; missing data and variable types processed in a 5-step pipeline; dataset split 80/20 into training/test sets; RF, XGBoost, LightGBM run to select significant predictors via variable importance, then compared via full-model vs. reduced-model prediction accuracy (rMSE) and training time; separately, a systematic literature review of 29 prior PISA predictive studies was conducted to identify 67 previously-reported predictors, top 10 ranked by frequency of citation.
column20: RF, XGBoost, and LightGBM each used to select significant predictors and evaluated via reduced- vs. full-model rMSE and training time (RQ1); ALE plots generated for the best model's (XGBoost's) selected predictors to visualize marginal, potentially non-linear relationships with math performance (RQ2); ML-selected predictors compared against literature-review-selected predictors via rMSE trends and a Wilcoxon signed-rank test (RQ3).
column21: RF selected 5 predictors; XGBoost and LightGBM each selected 10, sharing the same top 5: math self-efficacy, ESCS, familiarity with math concepts, expected occupational status, and family support for self-directed learning. XGBoost performed best overall (lowest error, fastest training), followed by LightGBM; RF had higher error and much longer training time. Plots showed math self-efficacy, ESCS, and math-concept familiarity positively linked to performance; family learning support, feelings about home learning, and math anxiety showed "moderate is best" patterns; paid work and exercise time were generally negative; expected occupational status and home ICT resources showed "too much or too little is bad" patterns.
column22: ML-based predictor selection is a more objective and accurate alternative to literature-review based selection, though less interpretable addressed here via ALE plots. Math self-efficacy, ESCS, and math anxiety were confirmed as key predictors, while ML also surfaced less commonly studied factors with nuanced, non-linear relationships. Findings offer practical guidance for instruction, interventions, curriculum, and policy in U.S. math education.
column23: The literature review (29 studies) may have inadvertently excluded some relevant papers despite a rigorous search strategy, an inherent LR limitation that could affect predictor comparison robustness.
column24: Employ additional literature-search strategies (e.g., citation tracking) for more exhaustive LR-based predictor identification; apply ML models to cross-national datasets to systematically compare math- performance predictors across countries, distinguishing universal from country-specific factors.
column25: Motivated by the U.S.'s lowest PISA math scores in two decades; compares 3 ML algorithms on accuracy and efficiency, and statistically quantifies how much more accurate ML-based predictor selection is than literature-review-based selection.

column2: Nitesh Kumar Jha; Meng-Jung Tsai
column4: Using Machine Learning Approaches to Predict Taiwanese Eighth Graders' Computational Thinking Performance in ICILS 2023 Study
column8: Computational thinking, machine learning, ICILS 2023, SHAP, ICT self-efficacy, CT disposition, secondary education
column11: ICILS 2023 Taiwanese 8th-grade data; IEA student questionnaire (132 variables) + national CT Disposition Scale (CTDS, 15 items); 18 features selected across three categories
column13: Logistic Regression (baseline), Random Forest, AdaBoost, XGBoost, LightGBM, Gradient Boosting, Stacking Ensemble; SHAP for feature importance
column14: Python (scikit-learn, XGBoost, LightGBM, hyperopt, optuna, SHAP)
column15: CT performance score (binary: below average vs. above average, threshold=541)
column16: 18 features: socio-demographic (5: sex, internet access, computer experience, home literacy, parent education), student-related (8: CTDS, ICT self-efficacy general/specialist, ICT attitudes, multitasking), school-related (5: specialist/general classroom apps, CT in class, internet tasks, safe use)
column17: To predict Taiwanese 8th graders' CT performance using ML models and identify the most important predictors across three variable categories.
column18:
1. Which ML model best predicts CT performance? 
2. What are the top-5 predictors across socio-demographic, student-related, and school-related variables?
column19: Multi-stage feature filtering (VIF-based multicollinearity check, IEA guidelines, theoretical relevance); 80/20 train-test split; 10-fold CV; hyperparameter tuning (hyperopt, optuna).
column20: Supervised binary classification (7 ML models); SHAP beeswarm plots for global feature importance; VIF for multicollinearity; model comparison via AUC, accuracy, precision, recall, F1.
column21: All ML models outperformed Logistic Regression (AUC=0.76). XGBoost and Stacking Ensemble achieved the best results (AUC=0.79, Accuracy=0.72). The single most important predictor across all 7 models was CT Disposition, students who approach problems systematically and persist through challenges score significantly higher in CT. Second and third were specialist ICT self-efficacy and general ICT self-efficacy, students confident in using digital tools perform better. The only school-level variable in the top 5 was exposure to specialist classroom applications, showing that curriculum-embedded digital tools matter. Academic multitasking was negatively associated, students who switch between tasks while using ICT tend to score lower. Gender and internet access at home had negligible effects.
column22: How a student thinks and approaches problems (CT disposition) is a stronger predictor of CT performance than their background or school environment. Students with higher digital self-confidence perform better regardless of gender or SES. School-level use of specialist applications provides meaningful support but alone is insufficient. Multitasking with ICT distracts students and harms performance, a finding specific to Taiwan that may reflect cultural differences. ML models reveal these nonlinear and interaction effects that logistic regression cannot capture. Overall, fostering CT mindset and digital self-efficacy should be prioritized over hardware provision.
column23: Single country and grade level; binary outcome loses score nuance; predictor interactions not modeled; no causal inference possible.
column24: Multi-country comparisons; multi-class CT scoring; SEM or XAI for interaction effects; inclusion of teacher support and learning habit variables.

column2: Yusuf Kasap and Mustafa Köro?lu
column4: The Effect of the Weight Variable on Predicting Reading Comprehension Achievement in PISA 2018: A Data Mining Approach
column8: Classification; sample weight; data mining
column11: Student-level data on reading comprehension achievement (PV1MATH-equivalent PV1 reading score, dichotomized) and 34 independent variables from the student questionnaire, analyzed with and without student-level sample weighting.
column13: CART and RF data mining methods; model evaluation via Correct Classification Rate (CCR/PCC), MAE, RMSE, Kappa coefficient, Relative Absolute Error (RAE), and Relative Root Squared Error (RRSE), computed on all data, 10-fold cross-validation, and test data
column14: SPSS Modeler (CART, RF classification/prediction); SPSS (outlier and missing-data analysis, multiple imputation); Weka (performance criteria calculation)
column15: Binary reading comprehension achievement (unsuccessful: PV1 score 0–552.999; successful: PV1 score 553–1000), based on the PISA 2018 Turkey national report's proficiency classification
column16: 34 variables: ESCS, index of highest parental occupational status, perceived difficulty of the PISA test, father's/mother's education, home possessions, ICT resources, family wealth, reading enjoyment, home educational resources, self-concept of reading, teacher's instructional orientation, student competition, teaching adaptation.
column17: To examine, as an original contribution to Turkish data mining literature (which had not previously incorporated sample weights), how including vs. excluding the student-level sample weight affects (a) which variables are identified as important predictors of PISA 2018 reading comprehension achievement in CART and RF models, and (b) classification/prediction performance of those models.
column18:
1. When the weight variable is considered in the CART model, how are the important variables predicting PISA achievement affected? 
2. When the weight variable is considered in the RF model, how are the important variables predicting PISA achievement affected? 
3. When the weight variable is included, how are the classification and prediction performances of the CART and RF models affected?
column19: Outlier and missing-data analysis conducted in SPSS; no outliers found, but missing data addressed via multiple imputation; PV1 selected as the dependent variable, dichotomized per the PISA 2018 Turkey national proficiency report; CART and RF run twice using the same 34 independent variables; top 10 important predictors identified per model; performance criteria then calculated separately on all data, 10-fold cross-validation data, and held-out test data.
column20: Parallel weighted vs. unweighted CART and RF models (4 total model runs) compared on: (a) identity and rank-order of the top 10 predictor variables (RQ1, RQ2), and (b) absolute (CCR, MAE, RMSE) and relative (Kappa, RAE, RRSE) performance metrics across all/validation/test data (RQ3).
column21: For CART, ESCS was the top predictor regardless of weighting, with only 1 of the top 10 variables differing between weighted/unweighted models. For RF, weighting had a larger, and the top predictor itself changed (reading enjoyment vs. teacher's instructional orientation); ESCS was not significant in either RF version. Both methods kept high, similar accuracy (83–86%) regardless of weighting, with only a slight non-significant drop when weighted. RF showed signs of overfitting (perfect on all-data, much weaker on validation/test), while CART stayed more consistently reliable.
column22: Sample weights matter for correctly identifying important predictors (especially in RF) but barely affect overall accuracy, even though prediction accuracy itself is barely affected. RF's overfitting makes CART more trustworthy for generalizable inference here. Socioeconomic factors consistently mattered in CART, while RF's failure to flag ESCS likely reflects known RF artifacts rather than a real absence of effect. The study concludes that sample weights are necessary for valid results in educational data mining, even if the accuracy cost of skipping them is small.
column23: No standalone limitations section; RF's overfitting (strong on all-data, weak on validation/test) is noted as a methodological caveat, and RF's variable-importance instability may partly reflect known algorithmic artifacts rather than substantive findings.
column24: Not detailed separately; the study implies continued use of sample weighting in future Turkish and international (TIMSS) data mining studies, and further investigation of RF's variable-importance instability.
column25: First Turkish data mining study to systematically use PISA sample weights, filling a gap in prior Turkish EDM literature; includes a worked example of how student-level sample weights are calculated; authors disclose no AI tools were used in writing the manuscript.

column2: Jiheng Wu, Baiwei Liu, and Qian Zhao
column4: Which Teachers Adopt AI in Teaching? An Interpretable Machine Learning Analysis of East Asian Data from TALIS 2024
column8: TALIS 2024; Artificial Intelligence; LASSO; Machine Learning
column9: Four East Asian economies (Singapore, Shanghai (China), Korea, and Japan).
column11: Teacher-level data on AI use in teaching (binary and frequency measures), work stress (composite and 3 sub-dimensions: workplace, workload, student-behavior stress), teaching enjoyment, professional development barriers, and teacher/school control variables
column13: LASSO (Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator) binomial logistic regression; AutoML (Automated Machine Learning; SHAP values; Fay-BRR weighted binary logistic regression
column14: R (packages: survey for weighted Logit models; glmnet for LASSO binomial regression; missForest for imputation); Python 3.10 with H2O for AutoML
column15: Teachers' AI adoption in teaching (binary: 1=used AI in teaching/to facilitate student learning in the past 12 months, 0=did not)
column16: Individual (age, teaching experience, work hours, teaching hours, workload stress, joy of teaching, personal/social utility motivations to teach, teaching self-efficacy, classroom management self-efficacy, perceived usefulness, perceived risk); Microsystem (teacher professional collaboration, instructional leadership, pedagogical support personnel ratio); Mesosystem (school socioeconomic status, school size, school autonomy)
column17: To identify, using interpretable machine learning (LASSO + AutoML/SHAP) guided by socio-ecological theory, the most important individual-, microsystem-, and mesosystem-level predictors of teachers' AI adoption across four East Asian TALIS 2024 economies (Singapore, Shanghai/ China, Korea, Japan), to compare how these predictors differ across economies, and to characterize nonlinear predictor-adoption relationships.
column18:
1. What are the most important predictors of teachers' AI adoption in teaching across East Asian TALIS 2024 samples?
2. How do these predictors differ across Singapore, Shanghai (China), Korea, and Japan?
3. What nonlinear relationships between key predictors and teachers' AI adoption are revealed through interpretable machine learning analysis?
column19: Countries classified as developed (OECD/high-income) vs. developing, with Shanghai treated separately; 4 exclusion steps applied to the original 278,383 observations (mainly due to gender-variable missingness in 30 countries), yielding the final 31,573-observation, 18-country sample; work stress computed as a factor score; school-clustered standard errors and fixed effects used throughout.
column20: Baseline OLS regression testing AI use => work stress and its 3 sub-dimensions, validated via weighted estimation, HLM, and propensity score matching; sub-sample regressions with interaction terms tested moderation by education level and national context; a 3-step mediation analysis tested teaching enjoyment and professional development barriers as parallel mediators
column21: AI use was significantly linked to lower overall work stress and all three sub-dimensions, robust across methods. The effect was significant only for non-postgraduate teachers, not postgraduates. By country context, AI use reduced stress in developing countries but increased it in developed countries. Mediation analysis showed AI use was linked to more teaching enjoyment and fewer professional development barriers; both mediated the AI-stress link, with teaching enjoyment playing the larger role.
column22: The AI-stress relationship is highly context-dependent, not uniformly beneficial: AI reduces stress for non-postgraduate teachers and in developing countries, but increases it in developed countries. This fits AI acting as both a resource (in resource-scarce contexts) and a new demand. Enhanced teaching enjoyment is the stronger mediating pathway. Policy should differentiate AI integration strategies by teacher group and national context.
column23: Cross-sectional design can't rule out reverse causality; unobserved factors could still confound results; mediation is statistical, not causal; all measures are self-reported; the binary AI-use measure misses frequency differences; the 18-country sample excludes major regions due to non-random missingness; the 3-category development classification may oversimplify.
column24: Use longitudinal data to clarify causality; expand to more diverse countries; develop more refined AI-use measures (frequency, scenarios, proficiency).
column25: Uses TALIS 2024's new AI module; grounded in Conservation of Resources theory and the Job Demands- Resources model; central finding is the "context-dependent reversal" between developing and developed countries.

column2: Huayu Shen and Tong Zhou
column4: Tools as Well-Being? AI Teaching Applications and Teacher Work Stress: Evidence From TALIS 2024
column8: TALIS 2024; artificial intelligence; AI teaching applications; teacher work stress; Job Demands- Resources model; Conservation of Resources theory
column11: Teacher-level data on AI use in teaching (binary and frequency measures), work stress (composite and 3 sub-dimensions: workplace, workload, student-behavior stress), teaching enjoyment, professional development barriers, and teacher/school control variables.
column13: OLS regression; robustness checks via BRR-weighted estimation, Hierarchical Linear Modeling (HLM), and Propensity Score Matching; sub-sample regression with interaction effects; three-step (Baron & Kenny-style) statistical mediation analysis
column15: Composite teacher work stress (factor score) and 3 sub-dimensions: workplace stress, workload stress, student behavior stress (original 4-point Likert scale scores)
column16: AI Teaching Applications (binary: used AI in teaching in past 12 months, yes/no; 56.12% "yes"), with Frequency of AI Teaching Applications as a robustness- check alternative; moderators: teacher educational attainment (postgraduate vs. non- postgraduate) and national development context; mediators: teaching enjoyment and professional development barriers
column17: To examine, using TALIS 2024's first-ever AI module, whether teachers' use of AI teaching applications is associated with reduced or increased work stress, whether this association is moderated by teachers' educational attainment and national development context, and whether it is statistically mediated by teaching enjoyment and professional development barriers.
column18: (H1a) AI teaching application use is negatively associated with teacher work stress. (H1b) AI use is positively associated with work stress. (H2) The AI-stress association varies by educational attainment, with a more pronounced stress-reducing effect among non-postgraduate teachers. (H3) The AI-stress association varies by national development level, stress-reducing in developing countries and potentially stress-amplifying in developed countries. (H4) The AI-stress association is statistically mediated by teaching enjoyment.  (H5) The AI-stress association is statistically mediated by professional development barriers
column19: Countries classified as developed vs. developing, with Shanghai treated as a separate category; 4 sequential exclusion steps applied to the original 278,383 observation TALIS 2024 dataset, yielding the final 31,573-observation, 18-country analytic sample; work stress composite computed as factor score, sub-dimensions/ mediators retained original Likert scale scores; school-level clustered standard errors and school fixed effects applied throughout to address teacher-within- school non-independence.
column20: Baseline OLS regression (with/without school fixed effects) testing AI use => work stress (and 3 sub-dimensions), validated via BRR-weighted estimation, HLM, and PSM (3 matching methods) as robustness checks; sub-sample OLS regressions plus interaction-effect models to test moderation by educational attainment (H2) and national development context (H3); three-step statistical mediation analysis testing teaching enjoyment and professional development barriers as parallel mediators (H4, H5)
column21: AI use significantly reduces overall work stress and its sub-dimensions (workload, workplace, and student behavior). However, this benefit varies heavily by group: it strongly reduces stress for non-postgraduate teachers, but has no significant effect on postgraduates. Crucially, the impact flips depending on national context. This stress reduction is primarily driven by increased teaching enjoyment and, to a lesser degree, fewer barriers to professional development.
column22: AI is not a universally beneficial tool for teachers; its impact is highly context-dependent. In developing countries, AI acts as a helpful job resource, whereas in already digitized developed countries, it acts as a new job demand that triggers technostress. Because of this, schools need tailored integration strategies. Resource limited regions and non-postgraduate teachers need standardized AI support and infrastructure, while developed regions and "technology pioneer" teachers need boundaries to protect against hidden workload and algorithmic overload.
column23: The study's cross-sectional design cannot prove causality, meaning teachers with lower stress might simply be more likely to adopt AI. Findings are also limited by self-reported data biases, unobservable traits (like natural tech enthusiasm), and a simple "yes/no" measure for AI use that ignores how often or how well the tools are used. Furthermore, missing data limited the final sample to only 18 of 55 countries, reducing global generalizability.
column24: Subsequent studies should use longitudinal data to confirm whether AI use directly causes a reduction in work stress over time. Researchers should also expand the sample to include more diverse educational systems and develop more nuanced AI metrics that track the specific frequency, application scenarios, and proficiency levels of the teachers using it.
column25: This study is notable for being the first to analyze cross-national AI outcomes using the newly introduced TALIS 2024 AI module. It effectively uses established job demand and resource theories to reframe AI as a dual-edged sword. Its most significant contribution is the "context-dependent reversal" finding, which shatters the assumption that AI lowers stress everywhere. The authors also explicitly disclosed using Claude for language editing.

column2: Ekaterina Enchikova, Tiago Neves, Cibelle Toledo, and Gil Nata
column4:
Change in socioeconomic educational equity after 20 years of PISA: A
systematic literature review
column5: International Journal of Educational Research Open
column8: Equity; Equality; PISA; SES; Segregation; Resilience
column9: Global (PISA-participating countries, with more coverage of OECD/European and some Latin American countries)
column11: Not a primary dataset; a synthesis of studies using PISA data across waves (2000–2022) reporting socioeconomic equity indicators at the country level
column13: None
column14: Endnote (duplicate identification), NVivo (full-text coding/review), Microsoft Excel and Tableau 2023.3 (data consolidation and visualization)
column15: Reported direction/trend of change in socioeconomic educational equity over time (coded as Positive, Negative, No change, Mixed, Unclear, Omit)
column16: Type of equity indicator (equality of opportunity, equality of outcome, resilience, segregation); PISA wave/year comparisons; country; PISA subject (reading, math, science, or mixed)
column17: To systematically review and synthesize independent studies and official PISA reports that quantitatively analyze change in socioeconomic educational equity over PISA's 20+ year history, summarizing methodological approaches and country-level results
column18:
1. What methodological approaches have been used to measure change in educational equity over time using PISA data? 
2. What results have been reported at the country level?
column19: PRISMA-based search across 3 databases in 2 rounds (2021, 2024); duplicates removed; two experts screened abstracts against 4 inclusion criteria (original quantitative PISA analysis, >=2 data points, specific languages); disagreements resolved by a third reviewer; results coded into 4 equity categories and 7 result types.
column20: Systematic review using a custom four-category equity framework (opportunity, outcome, resilience, segregation), combining UNESCO/OECD frameworks with patterns in the literature; results visualized by country and region.
column21: Equality of opportunity was the most studied dimension (26/38), followed by outcome (10), segregation (9), and resilience (3). Germany, UK, Mexico, and Denmark showed the most consistent positive trends; several Latin American countries also showed positive trends, though driven by few authors. Many high-equity European countries (Finland, Sweden, Iceland) showed negative trends despite already equitable systems. PISA 2022 indicated a general post-pandemic worsening of equality of outcomes. No clear consistent global trend emerged.
column22: Twenty years after PISA's start, countries have largely failed to achieve consistent equity improvements. The four equity categories lack a clear theoretical framework linking them, and inconsistent results often stem from differing methods, time frames, and a frequent lack of objective statistical criteria for classifying trends. The review distinguishes equity trends from equity levels, a country can be highly equitable yet show a negative trend, or vice versa.
column23: Findings reflect trends, not absolute equity levels; coding without objective statistical criteria required subjective interpretation; geographic coverage biased toward OECD/European countries; some country conclusions driven by very few studies.
column24: Develop a theoretical framework linking the four equity dimensions; study the reliability and validity of equity indicators; investigate the post-pandemic decline in equality of outcomes; clarify whether segregation should be interpreted alongside school enrollment/coverage rates.

column21: Stacking achieved the best performance, followed by XGBoost and RF, ANN performed moderately; LASSO and MLR performed weakest. Ensemble methods showed more stable performance across folds than linear models. Friedman/Wilcoxon tests confirmed Stacking and XGBoost significantly outperformed linear methods, with no significant differences among Stacking, XGBoost, and RF. Residual diagnostics showed ensemble/ANN models had more balanced error structures than linear models, which showed stronger heteroskedasticity. ESCS was the top predictor across all methods except ANN; RF and XGBoost were highly similar; ANN diverged most from other methods.
column22: Ensemble methods outperformed linear regression for modeling complex educational data, consistent with prior literature on boosting/bagging advantages. ESCS's consistent dominance as top predictor reinforces the well-documented role of socioeconomic status in achievement, while math self-efficacy and disciplinary climate highlight the joint importance of individual beliefs and classroom environment. ANN's divergent rankings suggest nonlinear models may capture interaction patterns linear/tree-based methods miss. Combining statistical and ML approaches for complementary insights and using ML models as potential diagnostic early-intervention tools in schools.
column23: Cross-sectional data precludes causal inference; PISA's complex sampling weights could not be fully integrated into predictive models, limiting national-level generalization; PVORT (mean of plausible values) does not capture individual-level uncertainty (Rubin's rules not applied); variable importance scores may be affected by measurement error in OECD-derived indices; restricted hyperparameter search spaces; ANN limited to a single hidden layer; stacking model, while accurate, had limited interpretability; different methods define variable importance differently, limiting direct numerical comparability.
column24: Employ longitudinal designs for causal inference; conduct cross-country comparative analyses; analyze plausible values separately and combine via Rubin's rules; explore multi-layer ANN architectures and broader hyperparameter ranges; apply explainability tools such as SHAP to improve interpretability of ensemble/stacking models; account for measurement error in derived indices when interpreting importance scores.

column19: Systematic review following Gough et al. (2017) 7-step protocol: search across 6 databases plus manual journal/reference screening; 5,268 records; 3,323 after deduplication; title/abstract screening against 4 inclusion criteria; 311 for full-text review; 82 final articles; coded across 88 variables in 6 themes (article info, data/sample, aims, STL variables, methods, results) by first author and research team, with disagreements resolved via discussion.
column20: Systematic review with narrative synthesis (not meta-analytic, due to non-comparable effect sizes across levels of analysis); studies grouped into three aim categories (relationships with outcomes; factors explaining STL variation; patterns of STL) and synthesized accordingly; methodological quality evaluated (sampling weights, plausible values, level of analysis, measurement invariance).
column21: Most articles (72/82) examined STL–outcome relationships: consistently positive for non-cognitive outcomes (enjoyment, attitudes, STEM interest), but mixed for achievement, unidimensional inquiry scales often showed negative associations, teacher-led activities positive, student-led investigations often negative, with some curvilinear relationships. Only 6 articles examined factors explaining STL variation; 8 examined STL patterns, finding meaningful cross-country differences. Methodological rigor varied widely, especially in sampling weights and plausible value use.
column22: TIMSS/PISA-based STL research complements small-scale studies but achievement findings remain inconsistent due to varying STL conceptualization and analytic level choices. Cross-sectional design limits causal inference; quasi-experimental studies found smaller effects than experimental meta-analyses. The review calls for more rigor, more research on STL variation/patterns, broader geographic representation, and better validation of self-report measures.
column23: Only peer-reviewed English-language articles included; narrative (not quantitative) synthesis due to incomparable effect sizes; STL items only crudely capture instructional quality; literature is geographically biased toward high-achieving Western/East Asian countries.
column24: Apply longitudinal/causal-inference methods; examine effects across subgroups; use computer-based log-file data; expand pattern and variation studies; include more Global South countries; validate STL items; link with TALIS; revise STL frameworks to cover underrepresented science practices.

Excellence and equity are context-dependent, not mutually exclusive.

column22: Findings support China's "Double Reduction Policy" by showing that excessive learning time does not improve (and can harm) academic performance beyond an optimal threshold, consistent with Carroll's learning time input theory. column19: Scales built from Likert-type items (4-point scales) with acceptable reliability (Cronbach's ?=0.752–0.809); teacher major coded binary (yes/no); group means compared by teacher gender via ANOVA; predictors entered simultaneously into multiple regression models for math and science.
column20: Multiple regression with five teacher-level predictors (practices, style, attitudes, experience, major) predicting math and science achievement separately; follow-up ANOVA comparing these variables between male and female teachers; correlation analysis between individual practice items and achievement, disaggregated by student gender.
column21: Regression models were significant for both math (R²=0.057) and science (R²=0.083); teachers' practices, teaching style, and teaching attitudes were the top three predictors in both subjects, with practices the strongest (partial R=0.180 for math, 0.206 for science). Female teachers scored significantly higher than male teachers on practices, teaching style, and attitudes (all p<0.01). Individual practice items correlated positively with achievement for both girls and boys. Saudi girls substantially outperformed boys nationally in both math and science.
column22: The gender achievement gap in Saudi Arabia may be partly explained by female teachers' more positive attitudes and stronger teaching practices/ style, consistent with similar international findings. Because Saudi Arabia uses single-sex schooling, it remains unclear whether female teachers would similarly benefit boys, unlike in mixed-gender contexts. Possible explanations include historically more selective entry into female teacher-training programs. For stronger teacher-selection standards and highlights ongoing Ministry of Education efforts as directions for improving male students' outcomes.
column23: Exploratory study; sample limited to 4th grade, so findings may not generalize to older students; other relevant teacher variables (enthusiasm, motivating style) were not examined; possible response-style differences between girls and boys evaluating same-gender teachers could not be tested since Saudi Arabia's single-sex system means boys only rate male teachers and girls only rate female teachers.
column24: Examine similar data from countries where boys rate female teachers and girls rate male teachers to test for response-style effects; include additional teacher variables such as enthusiasm and motivating teaching style; follow up with further studies examining teacher, school, and school-assignment variables to build a fuller explanation of the gender achievement gap in Saudi Arabia.
column25: First study to examine teacher characteristics (not just student gender) as predictors of the TIMSS achievement gap in Saudi Arabia's unique single-sex schooling context; findings carry direct implications for teacher recruitment and training policy at Saudi Arabia's Ministry of Education.

2. Which variables significantly affect mathematics literacy in each country? 
3. What is the relative order of importance of these variables per country?

column19: PV2MATH selected as dependent variable (highest correlation among 10 plausible values); M5P decision trees built per country; results validated via ANN on the same data, split into 70% training, 15% test,15% validation sets per country; consistency assessed via R^2, RMSE, and correlation between predicted and actual scores.

column21: ESCS was the top predictor in all countries except Japan (where math learning time was top, with father's education second). Second-level predictors varied: total learning time (Norway, USA, Turkey), teacher fairness/SSI (Singapore), out-of-school learning time (Norway), belonging to school (Dominican Republic). ANN prediction consistency was: Singapore 92.8%, USA 62.6%, Japan 56.1%, Norway 54.9%, Dominican Republic 54.3%, Turkey 51.4%. Correlation between actual and predicted scores was strongest for Norway among the M5P models, but ANN showed Singapore had by far the strongest correspondence.
column22: The predictors of mathematics literacy differ meaningfully by country and proficiency level, though SES is nearly universal as the top predictor. Country-specific explanations were offered: Singapore's history of poverty-reduction policy and strong teacher-quality investment likely explain the roles of SSI and teacher fairness; Norway's high education spending and low child poverty explain SSI's dominance and the role of motivation; the USA's large socioeconomic disparities align with existing literature on inequality's role in achievement gaps; results for Turkey diverged from prior PISA-2012-based studies, suggesting method- or cycle-specific differences.
column23: Not explicitly stated as a separate section; implicit limitations include the relatively low/moderate predictive consistency for most countries (R^2 26–43% for M5P models except Singapore), and the restriction to 15 pre-selected variables that may not capture all relevant predictors.
column24: Not explicitly detailed as a separate standalone section, though the paper implies further research is needed to explain the divergence from prior PISA-cycle studies (e.g., Turkey) and to explore additional variables or refine models for countries with lower prediction consistency.
column25: Distinctive for combining two independent methods (M5P decision trees and artificial neural networks) to cross-validate predictor findings across 6 countries spanning the full PISA proficiency range (Level 0 to Level 4); offers a comparative, cross-national data-mining approach rather than a single-country analysis.

column18:
1. Can accurate predictive models be built for individual students' maths anxiety status using a large set of background/context variables? 
2. What are the key predictors of maths anxiety identified by these models, and what are their educational implications?
column19: Missing data handled via multiple imputation (mice, 10 replications); maths anxiety dichotomized at 1 SD below the mean; 70/30 train-test split; random forest hyperparameters tuned via grid search (ntree 500–2500, mtry 10–26); classification threshold set at 0.3 (rather than default 0.5) after evaluating a range of thresholds.
column20: Three parallel prediction models fit on the same data: logistic regression, HGLM (two-level, accounting for school clustering), and random forest; models compared via accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, and AUC; variable importance examined via z-statistics (regression models) and accuracy/Gini-impurity importance plots (random forest).
column21: All three models achieved good accuracy and similar AUC (0.85), though random forest had higher sensitivity than the regression models. Logistic regression and HGLM identified nearly identical top predictors: negative self-concept, attributions to failure, lower enjoyment of maths, and being female were the strongest predictors; counterintuitively, participation in maths extracurricular activities, intentions to study maths, and parental/ teacher pressure to work hard were positively associated with anxiety. Random forest's accuracy-based importance favored interest/work-ethic/motivation variables and lack of self-control; its Gini-based importance favored ICT use, SES, and familiarity with maths concepts. Self-concept, attributions to failure, and enjoyment of maths were consistently selected.
column22: Random forest did not outperform regression-based models overall but achieved comparable accuracy and higher sensitivity without needing to explicitly model the hierarchical data structure, making it a viable alternative. Different models surfaced different predictor sets, suggesting combining multiple models offers a more complete picture of maths anxiety. Findings point to a "big-fish-little-pond effect" and social, parental, teacher pressure, rather than pure intrinsic motivation, as drivers of anxiety in Korea's high-stakes academic culture, and recommend interventions targeting self-confidence, perceived success, and reduced social pressure, ideally starting early in schooling.
column23: Model sensitivity remained relatively low despite good overall accuracy and AUC, consistent with prior machine-learning prediction research on at-risk students, likely due to the relatively low prevalence of maths anxiety in the sample; R² for educational survey-based prediction models is typically limited by a deficit of fully relevant input variables.
column24: Explore more relevant predictors of maths anxiety to improve overall accuracy and, especially, sensitivity; develop more precise prediction models; further investigate combining multiple prediction models to leverage their complementary strengths.
column25: Distinctive for applying and directly comparing three prediction paradigms (traditional regression, multilevel regression, and random forest) to the same large PISA-based predictor set (194 variables) in a single country; explicitly frames Korea's paradoxical pattern of high math achievement paired with high math anxiety as a context-specific, social-pressure-driven phenomenon distinct from Western literature.

column18:
1. Which profiles of students' inquiry performance can be identified from the two PISA 2015 items using exploration behavior, inquiry strategy, time-on-task, and item accuracy? 
2. To what extent do students' demographic characteristics, attitudes, and scientific literacy achievement differentiate their profile membership on the two items? 
3. How are profile memberships on the two items related (how many students share the same vs. different profiles across items)?
column19: Log files parsed into behavioral indicators (number of actions, number of trials, time before first action, response time); continuous indicators standardized; LCA/LPA fit sequentially from 1 to 5 classes per item; entropy and likelihood-ratio tests used to select the best-fitting (3-class) solution for both items; covariates (demographics, attitudes) added via LCA regression.
column20: Two-step latent profile analysis: (1) derive latent profiles per item from behavioral/accuracy indicators (LCA fit comparison across 1–5 classes); (2) regress profile membership on demographic/attitudinal/achievement covariates (multinomial logistic-style odds ratios) and examine cross-item profile transitions via chi-square/Cramér's V.
column21: 3-class solution fit best for both items, yielding "strategic, emergent, and "disengaged" profiles. Strategic students had the highest probability of using the correct strategy and solving items correctly; emergent students explored most but were less successful, especially on harder item; disengaged students explored least and never used the target strategy. Boys had higher odds of being disengaged; higher SES and self-efficacy/enjoyment reduced odds of being emergent/disengaged; non-Norwegian home language and test anxiety increased odds of being emergent. Profile memberships across items were related but only moderately stable, with just 38.7% consistently strategic.
column22: Log-file data revealed richer performer types than accuracy alone. Strategic students adapted by investing more time as task complexity increased; emergent students likely lacked the metacognitive knowledge to transfer strategies to harder tasks; disengaged students' pattern reflected motivational rather than cognitive factors, consistent with their higher anxiety and lower enjoyment/self-efficacy. Even high performers struggled to coordinate theory and evidence on the more complex task.
column23: Not explicitly detailed as a separate section within the excerpted text; the study is based on a single country's (Norway's) sample from a single assessment unit (two items), which may limit generalizability to other contexts, task types, or PISA cycles.
column24: Not explicitly detailed as a separate section within the excerpted text; findings point toward further investigation of metacognitive/ metastrategic knowledge in strategy transfer, motivational/attitudinal contributors to disengagement, and cross-national or cross-task replication using PISA log-file data.
column25: Distinctive for combining PISA's "process" (log-file/behavioral) data with traditional "product" (accuracy) data via latent profile analysis to characterize qualitatively different inquiry performance patterns, rather than relying on accuracy scores alone; contributes methodologically to the growing literature on using computer-based assessment log files to understand the "how" behind student performance, not just the "what".

column19: Google Trends queried using topic codes (language-agnostic) rather than raw search terms for PISA, TIMSS, and PIRLS; searches restricted to the "education" category; comparisons made either across countries or over time, since Google Trends cannot do both simultaneously; narrow time windows around simultaneous result releases used for direct comparisons.
column20: Descriptive comparison of Google Trends "popularity scores" (i) between ILSAs during overlapping release windows, (ii) across countries over 2006–2018/2020, and (iii) over time globally and within six large OECD countries (US, UK, Japan, Turkey, France, Germany); Spearman correlations tested co-occurrence of attention across ILSAs by country.
column21: PISA received roughly 10x more Google searches than TIMSS and far more than PIRLS (84% PISA, 12% TIMSS, 4% PIRLS); Saudi Arabia was the main exception (76% TIMSS). Estonia showed the highest relative interest in PISA, followed by Austria, Peru, and Germany; UK, US, Australia, Ireland, Canada, NZ showed comparatively low PISA interest despite high policy salience. TIMSS/PIRLS attention concentrated in Bahrain, Oman, Palestine, Jordan, UAE. Global PISA interest peaked with the 2012 results and has generally declined since, though with country-level exceptions (rising in Sweden, Turkey; falling in Germany, Japan, Spain, Italy, Netherlands). Cross-ILSA attention correlated modestly.
column22: This is the first study to quantify PISA's outsized attention relative to TIMSS/PIRLS, suggesting disproportionate influence over global education debate despite no clear methodological reason for this dominance. Global peak interest in PISA appears to have passed, though with substantial cross-country heterogeneity. Perceptions that ILSAs are especially prominent in Anglophone countries may be overstated relative to Central Europe. Continued innovation is needed to sustain relevance; IEA/OECD could raise TIMSS/PIRLS's profile so evidence is used more holistically.
column23: Google search volume is only one proxy for "attention" and doesn't identify who is searching (general public vs. policymakers/ researchers); Google's market share is lower in some countries of interest (China 4%, Russia 48%), limiting generalizability there; limited ability to link attention directly to score changes given constrained country/timepoint data.
column24: Further explore the relationship between country performance/score changes and the attention ILSAs receive as more data become available; investigate why PISA specifically garners disproportionate attention (branding, OECD's global profile, "real-world" skills framing); explore whether IEA/OECD efforts to elevate TIMSS/PIRLS profile succeed in balancing global ILSA discourse.
column25: Methodologically novel: first application of Google Trends data to systematically compare attention across ILSAs, countries, and time (rather than relying on newspaper-coverage case studies as prior literature did); offers a critical, cross-national quantitative counterpoint to prior single-country/single-ILSA qualitative studies of PISA's political and media impact.

1. What are the patterns of between- and within-school achievement inequality for a country across five cycles? 
2. Are schools becoming more unequal over time (increasing between-school inequality)?

column19: Schools with fewer than 10 tested students excluded; five PVs per student used, with analyses computed independently for each PV then averaged; total student weights applied for national representativeness; school-level mean scale scores computed via weighted averaging across PVs; between-school variance computed; within-school variance obtained by subtracting between-school variance from total weighted variance; Gaussian mixture modeling applied per school per PV, with optimal number of Gaussians then averaged across the 5 PVs
column20: Variance decomposition of science achievement into between-school and within-school components per country/cycle/grade, visualized via Between:Within SD ratios; correlation analysis between within-school average achievement and within-school inequality (SD); Gaussian mixture modeling to detect bimodality/multimodality in within-school score distributions, correlated with within-school average achievement.
column21: Between-school variance stayed largely stable across the 5 cycles for most countries, showing no clear rise in between-school inequality. Within-school inequality was consistently larger than between-school inequality, especially at Grade 4, though it grew somewhat by Grade 8 even in tracking systems. Higher-achieving schools showed lower within-school inequality than lower-achieving schools (sometimes 2–3× lower): lower-achieving schools were more likely to contain distinct student subpopulations, especially at Grade 4, with signs of rising heterogeneity by 2019.
column22: There's little evidence that between-school inequality has grown over two decades; within school inequality is the larger, more persistent driver of total inequality. The negative link between school achievement and within-school inequality supports a "virtuous" rather than "vicious" efficiency equality trade-off. Findings question the effectiveness of academic tracking, since within-school inequality stayed substantial even in tracking systems. Persistent bimodality in lower-achieving schools points to distinct student subpopulations needing differentiated instruction and targeted teacher training.
column23: Most schools sampled only 1–2 classes, limiting decomposition of within-school variance; comparability across 16 years may be affected by unmeasured changes; analysis was limited to science and didn't examine SES or other correlates; the 10-country sample doesn't represent broader regions.
column24: Identify correlates of inequality (SES, school characteristics); replicate in other subjects like math; use longitudinal data to clarify mechanisms linking bimodality and tracking; test whether homogenization in high-achieving schools affects student well-being; distinguish skewed-tail vs. bimodal inequality models.
column25: Uses TIMSS across five cycles (2003–2019) with an exploratory, non-hypothesis-testing design; combines variance decomposition with Gaussian mixture modeling to detect within-school bimodality.

column18: Framed as two competing hypotheses: H1) GERM governance tools (autonomy, leadership, accountability) improve performance and reduce achievement gaps by family background; H2) governance tools fail to reduce (or increase) the influence of socioeconomic background, so schools reproduce rather than remedy social inequality.
