column21: In both countries and all three years, ESCS was by far the strongest predictor of PISA science scores; governance tools added minimal explanatory power and showed inconsistent, often negative or non-significant effects. In Sweden, the ESCS effect rose sharply and earlier than in Finland, remaining high through 2015; disciplinary climate's effect also grew substantially, indicating rising school segregation. In Finland, ESCS effects grew too, approaching Sweden's levels by 2015. Migration variables showed weak effects except home language match, a modest positive predictor in both countries. Hypothesis H1 was refuted in all six models; Hypothesis H2 was confirmed in all six.
column22: Neither Sweden's radical marketization nor Finland's moderate decentralization reforms improved performance or reduced the socioeconomic achievement gap, family background's influence increased over time, more strongly and earlier in Sweden. Findings challenge OECD/GERM claims that autonomy plus accountability improves equity, and call for rethinking the global reform agenda given intensified school competition and standardized testing's potential downsides.

column24: Replicate analysis using TIMSS and PIRLS data, additional countries, and additional PISA test years; incorporate other structural, cultural, and governance-specific factors; examine parents'/students' strategies for benefiting from student-centered governance tools (achievement-based school choice, "cream skimming") to further test Hypothesis H2.

Reading ability also appears to influence mathematics achievement, consistent with prior research. column17: To empirically test a theoretical model of how education digitization affects student-perceived educational effectiveness, both directly and indirectly via teaching behavior and learning level, and to test whether grade and gender moderate these relationships.
column18: Framed as 12 hypotheses: H1) digitization level directly affects educational effectiveness; H2-H4) digitization level affects effectiveness indirectly via teaching behavior, learning level, and both in chain-mediation; H5-H8) grade level moderates these direct/indirect paths; H9-H12) gender moderates these direct/indirect paths.
column19: Questionnaire items selected from PISA 2022 ICT questionnaire (IC172, digitization construction), student questionnaire (digitization application; learning level; teaching behavior; educational effectiveness); cases with missing/invalid/ inapplicable data removed, yielding 53,908 valid samples; KMO/Bartlett tests confirmed suitability for factor analysis; reliability/ validity of each scale assessed as good.
column20: PLS-SEM: measurement model fit assessed via goodness-of-fit indices (SRMR, NFI, chi-square); structural model tested via bootstrapping (5,000 resamples) for path coefficient significance; multigroup (bootstrap) analysis conducted separately for grade-level and gender subgroups to test moderation hypotheses.
column21: Digitization level had no significant direct effect on educational effectiveness. However, digitization significantly and positively affected effectiveness indirectly via teaching behavior, via learning level, and via a chain mediation through both teaching behavior and learning level. Grade level significantly moderated the direct and indirect paths, with stronger effects for lower-grade students (H5, H6, H8 supported). Gender significantly moderated all tested paths (H9–H12 supported), consistent with the hypothesis that digital technology's influence differs by gender.
column22: Digitization alone does not automatically improve perceived educational effectiveness. Instead, digitization's benefits are realized indirectly, by shaping how teachers teach and how students behave in the classroom, with a particularly strong chain effect through both teaching behavior and learning level together. Lower-grade students and certain gender groups are more strongly affected, suggesting digitization strategies should be differentiated by age and possibly by gender-sensitive design. Policy focus on teacher digital competency and student engagement rather than infrastructure alone.
column23: Educational effectiveness was measured via a single self-perceived item (quality of math teaching), which the authors acknowledge is a limited (though defensible) proxy; actual grades, emotional/attitudinal outcomes, and other effectiveness indicators were not included; findings are specific to basic education given PISA's target population and may not generalize to higher education, which differs in learning autonomy, content, and digital implementation strategies; other unmeasured moderating variables were not tested.
column24: Incorporate additional effectiveness measures using questionnaires, structural equations, big data, interviews, and case studies; more comprehensively model and measure "learning level" via classroom observation, interviews, and case studies; investigate additional moderating variables; extend or adapt the model and data collection to higher-education contexts for comparison.
column25: Explicitly situates its findings within China's national "digitization of education" policy agenda while using global PISA 2022 data; notable for demonstrating that digitization's effect on perceived educational quality is entirely indirect (mediated through teacher and student behavior) rather than direct, with a full theoretical model proposing 12 hypotheses tested via PLS-SEM.

column20: SVM-RFE used to rank all contextual variables by classification relevance; three candidate optimal feature sets (top 10, 20, 30) compared for prediction accuracy via SVM classifier and 10-fold cross-validation; top 20 features selected as optimal set and validated via two additional rounds of 10-fold cross-validation (accuracy/recall).
column21: The top 20 feature set achieved the best balance of minimal features and maximum accuracy. Cross-validation confirmed good performance. The most predictive features included: teacher feedback and adaptive instruction, teacher-directed teaching and support, parents' high education level and occupational status, disciplinary climate, in/out-of-school learning time, school ICT access, inquiry-based teaching, instructional time for science, low student-teacher ratio, early childhood education attendance, science-related activity participation, and science self-efficacy.
column22: The SVM-based approach successfully identified a compact, high-accuracy set of contextual predictors spanning student, family, and school levels, largely reinforcing prior theoretically-driven findings via a data-driven, machine-learning lens. Findings were also interpreted through educational productivity theory (instruction, aptitude, social-psychological environment categories), reinforcing the importance of instructional quality, parental socioeconomic status, and student affective/motivational factors in producing top science performers.
column23: All features are descriptive/correlational rather than causal or objectively measured; data relied on students' self-reported questionnaire responses, raising data-quality concerns; the SVM/SVM-RFE approach captures variable inter-relatedness implicitly but does not visualize impact direction/magnitude as structural equation modeling might; SVM methods carry high computational load, parameter-tuning expertise requirements, and reliance on costly cross-validation for interpretation.
column24: Integrate more objective (non-self-report) survey measures in future PISA cycles; conduct longitudinal studies with more reliable data collection to address self-report limitations; apply complementary statistical methods (e.g., structural equation modeling) to reveal mediating effects and directional relationships among the identified features.
column25: One of the earlier applications of SVM/SVM-RFE (rather than decision trees, the more common ML approach in PISA research) to identify top-performer profiles across a very large, multi-country PISA 2015 sample (380,771 students, 58 countries); explicitly compares its ML approach against classification and regression trees (CART), a more commonly used method in prior PISA data-mining studies.

column20: Scoping literature review following the Arksey and O'Malley (2005) framework; results organized and compared across the nine ICT context variables, summarizing patterns in reported associations (positive/negative/null) with math and science achievement across studies, countries, and PISA cycles.
column21: The relationship between ICT and academic achievement was inconsistent across studies, varying by ICT type, subject, and country. Moderate ICT use (rather than high or no use) tended to positively predict achievement. Less-studied variables tended to positively predict both math and science scores, though they were less frequently examined than usage-based variables. AUTICT showed no negative or null relationships in the reviewed literature; SOIAICT showed no null relationships. SES and school type moderated some ICT-achievement relationships (low-SES students benefited more from increased home ICT use, while mid-to-high-SES low-frequency users benefited more from increased school ICT use).
column22: There is a lack of overall consensus on ICT's relationship with achievement, underscoring that context (country, subject, SES, school type) fundamentally shapes these relationships. A research gap exists around the "softer" ICT measures (competence, interest, autonomy) relative to the heavily studied "use" measures. Policymakers and educators should promote the specific ICT interactions shown to positively predict achievement while limiting those with negative associations, and should avoid designing curricula solely to boost PISA rankings, since rankings can be misleading and subject to overinterpretation.
column23: Practical: not as comprehensive as a full systematic review; constrained by the limited number of published studies. Methodological: all included studies are correlational/cross-sectional; ICT Familiarity Questionnaire lacks detail on device quality or meaningfulness of use; no measures of teacher/parent ICT skill are available as covariates; measurement invariance across countries is not established; ICT measures are self-reported; PISA's sample.
column24: Use theoretical reasoning to select appropriate covariates/control variables rather than over-controlling; replicate studies across the same countries in new PISA iterations to examine change over time; adopt mixed-methods approaches for deeper understanding of ICT interactions; build explanatory models accounting for country- and subject-specific differences with appropriate confounders; expand focus on understudied "softer" ICT constructs.
column25: A scoping (not systematic) review explicitly following Arksey and O'Malley's (2005) framework, intended to map the variety and inconsistency of findings rather than provide an exhaustive or quality-appraised synthesis; frames ICT effects through self-determination theory, linking non-cognitive ICT-related factors (autonomy, competence, interest) to cognitive achievement outcomes; explicitly critiques the use of PISA rankings as a policy-driving metric.

column20: Three-part analysis: (1) CFA + measurement invariance testing to validate instructional quality factor structure across countries/cycles (RQ1); (2) descriptive statistics and one-way ANOVA to test within-country mean differences in SES and instructional quality across the two cycles (RQ2); (3) SEM examining direct and SES-mediated indirect effects of instructional quality dimensions on mathematics achievement (RQ3).
column21: In PISA 2012, teacher support, disciplinary climate, and cognitive activation positively predicted achievement, while student-oriented instruction and classroom management were negatively related in several countries. In PISA 2022, teacher support and disciplinary climate again positively predicted achievement, but the two cognitive activation sub-dimensions had opposite effects. SES had significant positive indirect effects on achievement through several instructional quality dimensions. Across both cycles, teacher support, disciplinary climate, and cognitive activation consistently benefited low-SES students.
column22: Instructional quality showed a stable, positive relationship with mathematics achievement over a decade across diverse European education systems, supporting the DMEE framework's relevance. SES remains a persistent and consistent predictor of achievement, both directly and indirectly through instructional quality dimensions; high-SES students appear to benefit more from high-quality instruction, reinforcing existing inequalities unless addressed. Findings support targeted interventions and teacher professional development as levers for improving equity for disadvantaged students.
column23: Not explicitly detailed as a standalone limitations section in the extracted text; implicit limitations include that only two of the original instructional quality scales (teacher support, disciplinary climate) could be validly trend-linked across the two PISA cycles, restricting some trend comparisons; instructional quality is based on student perceptions rather than observed/actual teaching.
column24: Refine PISA's instructional quality measures in future cycles, potentially reintroducing or improving trend-comparable dimensions of classroom management and student-oriented instruction; continue investigating targeted, equity-focused interventions for disadvantaged (low-SES) students across educational systems.
column25: Distinctive for its decade-long (2012–2022), 10-country trend analysis of instructional quality within the DMEE theoretical framework, combining CFA/measurement invariance, ANOVA trend testing, and SEM mediation analysis in a single study; explicitly ties findings to policy implications for teacher professional development and SES-related equity interventions.

column20: Six-step procedure: (1) data collection, (2) country split, (3) RF-based feature selection, (4) ARF algorithm application to identify high-achievement student subsets via recursive splitting (H criterion), (5) results interpretation, (6) cross-country comparison.
column21: 47% of Turkish and 58% of Chinese students scored above their respective country averages. ARF identified 5 distinct high-achievement subgroups in each country. In Turkey, the top subset (91% success rate) was defined by high metacognition combined with high ESCS (top 15%). In China, the top subset (95% success rate) was defined by high METASPAM, high ESCS, and moderate science learning time. Variable importance ranking showed metacognition and ESCS were the top two predictors in both countries, though subsequent predictors diverged.
column22: Metacognitive competence and ESCS are the most universally important drivers of high reading achievement across both countries, suggesting curriculum reform should prioritize these skills. Country-specific factors (ICT use in Turkey; test-difficulty perception, reading enjoyment, and science learning time in China) point to differentiated policy priorities. Consistent with GDP disparities ($9,126 Turkey vs. $20,000 China per capita), the authors recommend Turkish policymakers pursue both economic development and educational curriculum reform to close the achievement gap.
column23: Not explicitly detailed as a standalone limitations section in the extracted text; implicit limitations include the ARF method's reliance on iterative rule-based splitting (interpretable but not a full predictive model) and the study's scope being limited to two countries.
column24: Not explicitly detailed as a standalone section; the paper implies further application of the ARF method to other PISA-participating countries and continued monitoring of curriculum reforms targeting metacognition and socioeconomic disparities.
column25: Introduces the Activity Region Finder algorithm as a novel application to educational large-scale assessment data, distinct from standard regression or classification-tree approaches; explicitly frames Turkey's PISA underperformance relative to China as a policy problem tied to both economic development and curriculum design.

column22: Cultural context shapes both the prevalence of instructional practices and, to some extent, their relationship with reading performance. Some relationships (positive effects of support instruction; negative effects of directed instruction/feedback) held across both Asian and Western regions, suggesting a degree of universality despite cultural differences in how common these practices are. Findings support socio-cultural theorizing and inform teacher education, curriculum reform, and cross-cultural policy transfer.
column23: Only the 10 top-performing PISA 2018 regions were included, excluding other Asian (Japan, Taiwan) and Western (US, UK) regions, limiting generalizability; student-level factors (reading enjoyment, self-efficacy, engagement) were not examined alongside instructional practices.
column24: Include a larger, more diverse sample of regions for better generalizability; incorporate student-level affective/ motivational factors (reading enjoyment, self-efficacy, engagement) alongside instructional practices; use qualitative methods (school observations, interviews) to explore within-region/national cultural nuances underlying exceptions to the general patterns.
column25: Distinctive for its deliberately diverse 10-region comparative design (avoiding the common single-country "China vs. America" proxy for Asian vs. Western culture); grounded explicitly in Sociocultural Theory and the PISA Teaching, Monitoring, Questioning Techniques framework to interpret cross-cultural patterns in instructional practice and reading achievement.

column21: ICT availability at home/school and virtually all forms of ICT use were negatively associated with math and science performance across most cycles. In contrast, positive ICT-related attitudes were consistently positively associated with performance across all four cycles. At the school level, number of computers per student showed no substantive association with performance, while proportion of computers connected to the internet showed generally positive associations (2015 math). ESCS remained the most substantive school-level predictor across cycles. School provision of extra-curricular activities showed a consistent positive association with performance; country GDP per capita showed no consistent association except in 2012.
column22: The volume/frequency of ICT use and availability (both at home and school) appears largely distracting for adolescent students and detrimental to math/science performance, contradicting a simple "more ICT=better outcomes" assumption, while positive attitudes toward and autonomous, purposeful use of ICT are what actually support achievement. Findings suggest schools and parents should focus on cultivating positive ICT attitudes and self-directed, purposeful technology use rather than simply expanding access or usage time. School connectivity (rather than raw computer counts) and extra-curricular activity provision are practical levers worth further attention.
column23: PISA's cross-sectional design precludes causal inference; ICT-related variables are self-reported, risking biased/exaggerated estimates of attitudes and use; the ICT questionnaire item set varied across cycles, potentially limiting comprehensive/ comparable measurement of ICT behavior; results are bound to the specific variables included (no teacher/parent ICT attitude or support measures).
column24: Use experimental or longitudinal designs to establish causal relationships; employ data collection methods that more precisely measure ICT use beyond self-report; incorporate additional ICT-related variables such as teacher and parental attitudes/support toward educational technology; investigate student ICT accessibility and attitudes during and after COVID-19-related schooling disruptions; further explore non-linear relationships between school ICT infrastructure and performance, and role of national ICT development level.

column13: Review-level synthesis; Qualitative Comparative Analysis and Necessary Condition Analysis
column15: N/A; across included studies, the outcome was PISA mathematics achievement score
column16: 135 identified factors across included studies, organized into 5 Bronfenbrenner ecological levels: individual student, household context, school community, education systems, and macro society (57 factors examined in >=5 studies)
column17: To systematically review and synthesize the factors found to predict PISA mathematics achievement across the existing peer-reviewed literature, organizing findings within Bronfenbrenner's ecological model of human development.
column18: Not formally numbered as RQs; the review's overarching aim was to comprehensively map factors predicting PISA math performance and identify which are consistently, tendentially, or inconsistently (mixed) associated with achievement.
column19: PRISMA 2020-guided search using 7 Boolean search strings across 5 databases, limited to English-language peer-reviewed articles; Rayyan used for initial relevance screening; inclusion criteria applied (peer-reviewed, English, PISA math score analysis, published in a journal that was Q1-ranked in Scimago at least once 2016–2020); dual/triple independent rater screening with inter-rater reliability checks (80% agreement); quality appraised via Johns Hopkins nursing evidence-based practice rating scale.
column20: PRISMA-based systematic review with narrative synthesis; factors coded and categorized into Bronfenbrenner's 5 ecological levels; each factor's association with math achievement classified as consistently positive, consistently negative, tending positive/negative (>=80% of studies), or mixed.
column21: 135 distinct factors were identified; 60% were examined in fewer than 5 studies. Among the 57 factors studied in >=5 papers, 2 were consistently positively associated with math achievement and 5 consistently negatively associated (student lack of punctuality, school repeating/dropout rate, school prevalence of student misbehavior, shortage of teachers/staff, student-centered instruction). An additional 14 factors tended positive and 2 tended negative (>=80% of studies agreeing); the remaining 36 factors showed mixed results. Gender was the most frequently studied factor (68 studies), followed by family SES (93 studies/60%).
column22: Math achievement is shaped by factors. Negative association between student-centered instruction and math achievement is notable and counter intuitive given global instructional trends, possibly reflecting math's technical nature requiring more teacher guidance, PISA test-takers' development stage, uneven measurement of "student centered" constructs across studies, or curriculum assessment misalignment. Mixed results for many factors likely reflect methodological heterogeneity, complex cross-variable interactions, and underlying national cultural or macro level moderators.
column23: English-language-only search may have missed non-English literature; only 5 electronic databases searched; Q1-journal ranking restriction likely excluded some high-quality non-Q1 studies and associated factors; despite high inter-rater reliability, some relevant studies could have been missed; comparability across studies is limited by varying measures, missing-data strategies, and confidence-interval thresholds; the 135-factor list is likely non-exhaustive; PISA's student/school-only identifiers preclude teacher-level analysis.
column24: Investigate education-system and macro-society level factors more thoroughly for cross-national understanding; use varied methodologies to study interactions among micro-meso-macro factors; apply longitudinal or experimental designs to test causality beyond PISA's cross-sectional data; conduct qualitative work to unpack cross-level mechanisms; extend systematic reviews to other PISA domains for comparison.
column25: First systematic review specifically focused on PISA mathematics achievement predictors (distinct from prior broader PISA reviews, ICT-focused reviews, or meta-analyses not specific to math/PISA); explicitly organizes the very large and fragmented predictor literature using Bronfenbrenner's ecological "person-process-context" model, providing a comprehensive reference framework for future PISA math research and policy.

column2: Demos Michael and Leonidas Kyriakides
column4: Mediating Effects of Motivation and Socioeconomic Status on Reading Achievement: A Secondary Analysis of PISA 2018
column8: Equity in education; socioeconomic status; academic motivation; international large-scale assessments; mediation analysis
column9: 38 European countries (of 41 European PISA 2018 participants, 3 excluded for insufficient data)
column11: Student-level data on reading achievement (10 plausible values), ESCS, and three academic motivation constructs (mastery-approach goal orientation, enjoyment of reading, expected occupational status).
column13: Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA) and Multiple Group CFA, Structural Equation Modeling
column15: Reading literacy achievement (10 plausible values, averaged across 10 model runs)
column16: SES (PISA ESCS index, z-scored); mediators: mastery approach orientation of achievement goals (3 items), enjoyment of reading (5 items), expected occupational status (open-ended item coded via ISCO/mapped to PISA ISEI)
column17: To examine whether and to what extent three academic motivation elements (mastery-approach goals, reading enjoyment, expected occupational status) mediate the relationship between SES and reading achievement across European PISA 2018 countries.
column18:
1. Which of the three academic motivation elements mediate the relationship between SES and reading achievement, and to what extent? 
2. To what extent can each of the three elements be treated as a mediator in each individual European country?
column19: Student sampling weights applied; ESCS z-scored for cross-country comparability; 10 plausible values for reading used, with analysis run 10 times and parameters averaged per OECD guidance; two-factor CFA models run separately per country (38 models) to validate mastery-goals and reading-enjoyment latent structures (expected occupational status treated as observed); MGCFA conducted to test measurement invariance across countries.
column20: Within-country CFA to validate mediator factor structure, followed by MGCFA to test cross country measurement invariance; full mediation SEM model (SES 3 motivation mediators reading achievement) tested separately in each of the 38 countries, with non-significant mediators trimmed and models re-fit for satisfactory fit.
column21: In 10 countries, all three mediators were statistically significant; in the remaining 28, only two fit well. Expected occupational status was a significant mediator in all 38 countries and had the largest mediating effect in 31 of them. Enjoyment of reading mediated in 37 of 38 countries. Mastery approach orientation of achievement goals mediated in only 11 countries, with no clear geographic, cultural, linguistic pattern explaining which countries. The direct effect of SES on reading achievement was substantially reduced after accounting for the mediators in every country, though SES retained a significant direct effect in all cases. The two significant mediators were positively correlated with each other countries.
column22: Expected occupational status and enjoyment of reading are robust, near-universal mediators of the SES-reading achievement relationship across Europe, supporting equity-focused interventions that target students' intrinsic reading motivation and educational aspirations, SES disadvantaged students. Mastery-approach goal orientation's more limited mediating role may partly reflect its narrower item-based measurement in PISA rather than a true absence of the underlying relationship, since factor loadings were strong in the 11 countries where it did emerge as a mediator. Practical implications include teacher led orientation and self-regulated learning tasks.
column23: Cross-sectional design precludes causal inference; only three academic motivation elements (constrained by available PISA items) were examined, and mastery approach goals were measured with only 3 items, potentially limiting theoretical completeness; enjoyment of reading is subject-specific while the other two mediators are more generic, complicating direct comparison; scope limited to European countries and 15-year-olds only.
column24: Conduct longitudinal studies to test predictive/causal mechanisms; investigate additional academic motivation elements as potential mediators; test whether the generic mediators operate similarly across other academic subjects; extend mediation analysis to non-European regions and other age groups; combine quantitative and qualitative approaches to understand context-specific mediation patterns.
column25: Notable for testing the same theoretical SES-motivation-achievement mediation model separately across 38 countries (rather than pooling data), revealing both highly consistent (expected occupational status, reading enjoyment) and highly variable (mastery-approach goals) mediation patterns; frames findings explicitly around equity-in-education policy implications for socioeconomically disadvantaged students.

column2: Ana María Suárez-Mesa and Ricardo L. Gómez
column4: Does Teachers' Motivation Have an Impact on Students' Scientific Literacy and Motivation? An Empirical Study in Colombia With Data From PISA 2015
column6: Web of Science and Google Scholar
column8: PISA; intrinsic motivation; self-determination theory; scientific literacy; Colombia
column11: Student-level scientific literacy scores (plausible values), student intrinsic motivation index, teacher motivation index, and student/teacher/school-level predictor variables for Colombia
column12: 8,095 students and 1,314 science teachers from 313 schools
column13: Two-level Hierarchical Linear Modeling (HLM); null models
column15: Students' scientific literacy (PISA science plausible values, M=500, SD=100); students' intrinsic motivation (composite index, M=0, SD=1)
column16: Level 1 (student): grade relative to modal grade, home educational resources, ICT resources, ESCS, interest in science, expected occupational status, grade repetition, self-efficacy in science, gender. Level 2 (teacher/classroom/ school): inquiry-based teaching, teacher-directed instruction, teacher support, school type (public/private), enrollment, class size, student/teacher behaviors affecting climate, school ESCS, and a composite teacher motivation index
column17: To investigate, using a multilevel modeling approach grounded in Self-Determination Theory, whether teachers' motivation affects students' scientific literacy and students' own intrinsic motivation in Colombia, controlling for individual and school-level variables.
column18: What is the effect of teachers' motivation on students' scientific literacy and motivation, after controlling for individual and school-level variables?
column19: Teacher-level data aggregated to the school level and merged into the student-level file per PISA multilevel analysis standards; 10 plausible values for scientific literacy used in the analysis; reliability of composite indices confirmed (student motivation ?=.853; teacher motivation ?=.85); null models computed to derive ICCs prior to full model specification.
column20: Two separate two-level HLM models: (1) predicting students' scientific literacy from Level 1 (student) and Level 2 (teacher/school) variables including teacher motivation; (2) predicting students' intrinsic motivation from the same variable set, including teacher motivation as a predictor.
column21: Teacher motivation showed no significant relationship with either students' scientific literacy or students' intrinsic motivation. Teacher-directed instruction was the strongest positive predictor of scientific literacy, while inquiry-based teaching showed no significant effect on literacy but did positively predict students' intrinsic motivation. Students' own interest in science and science self-efficacy were significant positive predictors of literacy. Grade repetition was strongly linked to lower literacy (non-repeaters scored 17 points higher per grade level, reflecting Colombia's vertical stratification system. For the motivation model, ICC was only 2%, and school SES showed a significant negative relationship with student motivation.
column22: Contrary to common policy assumptions, teacher motivation showed no significant direct association with either student achievement or student motivation in this Colombian sample; instead, specific teaching strategies (teacher- directed instruction, inquiry-based teaching) and students' own interest/self-efficacy were the stronger predictors. Findings support continued investment in improving teaching strategies and classroom support rather than assuming teacher motivation alone drives outcomes, though the authors caution that teacher motivation could still matter through unmeasured mediating pathways (competence, relatedness, autonomy fulfillment) worthy of further study.
column23: Cross-sectional design precludes causal inference; teacher motivation was operationalized via job satisfaction, a related but distinct construct from motivation, limiting interpretive precision; available data could not test moderating/mediating pathways (absenteeism, turnover) linking motivation to learning; findings are specific to Colombia and 2015 PISA cycle.
column24: Conduct longitudinal or experimental studies to test causal relationships between teacher motivation and student outcomes; develop more unified, validated constructs and instruments for measuring teacher intrinsic motivation (beyond job satisfaction proxies); expand data collection to include teacher behaviors/attitudes that may mediate or moderate the motivation-learning relationship, especially in emerging/ developing economies.
column25: Notable for directly testing (and largely refuting) the common policy assumption that teacher motivation drives student outcomes in a developing-country context, using PISA data through a Self-Determination Theory lens; highlights Colombia-specific structural factors (vertical grade stratification/ repetition) as a major, often overlooked achievement predictor.

column2: Allan B. I. Bernardo and Ma. Joahna Mante-Estacio
column4: Metacognitive Reading Strategies and Its Relationship With Filipino High School Students' Reading Proficiency: Insights From the PISA 2018 Data
column6: Web of Science and Google Scholar
column8: N/A
column11: Student-level data on reading proficiency (overall and 3 cognitive subscales, plausible values), 11 self-reported metacognitive reading strategy usefulness ratings, ESCS, number of books at home, and sex
column13: Repeated-measures ANOVA with Bonferroni post-hoc comparisons (strategy usefulness ratings); four hierarchical multiple regression analyses (overall reading proficiency + 3 cognitive subscales)
column15: Overall PISA 2018 reading proficiency and three cognitive subscales: locate information, understand, evaluate and reflect (all first plausible value)
column16: Perceived usefulness ratings (1–6 scale) of 11 metacognitive reading strategies (6 for understanding/memorizing, 5 for summarizing); control variables: sex, ESCS, number of books at home
column17: To examine how Filipino 15-year-old students' perceived usefulness of 11 metacognitive reading strategies relates to their overall reading proficiency and its three cognitive subscales in PISA 2018, given the Philippines' last-place ranking in reading among participating countries.
column18:
1. What strategies are perceived to be more useful by Filipino high school students? 
2. What strategies are associated with Filipino high school students' total reading proficiency and with each of the three cognitive subscales of reading proficiency?
column19: Analysis restricted to students with complete data on all main and control variables (final N=6,591); distribution/ correlation checks confirmed the 10 plausible values were nearly identical, justifying use of the first plausible value; repeated-measures ANOVA conducted for strategy usefulness comparison; hierarchical regression conducted separately for overall proficiency and each cognitive subscale, entering control variables (Step 1) then the 11 strategies (Step 2).
column20: Repeated-measures ANOVA (with Bonferroni post-hoc) to rank strategies by perceived usefulness (RQ1); four hierarchical regression analyses (overall proficiency, locate information, understand, evaluate/reflect) adding the 11 metacognitive strategies after controlling for sex, ESCS, and books at home (RQ2).
column21: Strategy usefulness ratings differed significantly; the top three strategies (underlining/note-taking) were rated most useful, while low-level strategies (copying, reading aloud) were rated least useful. Adding the 11 strategies to the regression model explained an additional 18% of variance in overall proficiency (14 some mid-ranked strategies were more strongly linked to proficiency, the two lowest-ranked strategies were negatively linked, and two showed no relationship. Basic-processing strategies related more to lower-order subscales than to higher-order evaluation.
column22: Filipino students show a gap between which strategies they perceive as useful and which actually predict proficiency, suggesting limited metacognitive awareness. This may reflect gaps in how reading strategies are taught in Philippine curricula, or students' own classroom experiences. Findings support more integrated strategy instruction, and suggest first-language reading skills likely also shape second-language reading proficiency
column23: Analysis used only three control variables, so relative importance versus other cognitive/family/school factors couldn't be tested; limited to the 11 strategies measured in PISA 2018, excluding other potentially relevant strategies.
column24: Analyze a wider range of factors and strategies beyond the PISA-measured set; study how reading strategies are actually taught in Philippine classrooms; explore how first language reading skills shape second language reading proficiency.
column25: Uses a nationally representative sample (unlike prior small-scale Filipino studies); frames the usefulness predictiveness mismatch as evidence of a metacognitive awareness gap tied to how reading strategies are taught.

column2: Virginia M. C. Tze, Johnson C.-H. Li, and Lia M. Daniels
column4: Similarities and Differences in Social and Emotional Profiles Among Students in Canada, USA, China, and Singapore: PISA 2015
column8: Social-emotional skills; latent profile analysis; cross-cultural comparison; standardised international student achievement
column9: Canada, United States, China, and Singapore
column11: Student-level data on four CASEL social-emotional competency indicators (derived from PISA questionnaire items) and reading, math, and CPS achievement (plausible values)
column13: Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA) and Multigroup CFA (MGCFA); Latent Profile Analysis (LPA); BCH approach (Bolck-Croon-Hagenaars)
column15: PISA 2015 reading, mathematics, and Collaborative Problem Solving (CPS) achievement scores (mean of 10 plausible values per domain)
column16: Four CASEL social-emotional competency indicators derived from PISA questionnaire items: self-awareness, self- management, social awareness, relationship skills; latent profile membership (country-specific)
column17: To determine whether CASEL's four social-emotional competencies could be validly compared across countries, to identify social-emotional skill profiles (SESP) among 15-year-olds in Canada, USA, China, and Singapore, and to evaluate how these profiles relate to reading, math, and CPS achievement.
column18:
1. Can a four-factor social-emotional skills model (based on CASEL competencies) be used for cross-national comparisons? 
2. What social-emotional profiles exist among 15-year-olds in Canada, USA, China, and Singapore, and are they most similar within Western (Canada-USA) vs. Asian (China-Singapore) country pairs? 
3. How do different social-emotional profiles predict students' reading, math, and CPS scores?
column19: CFA conducted per country to validate the four-factor structure; MGCFA tested configural, factor-loading, and threshold invariance across the four countries (CFI<0.01 criterion); LPA conducted separately per country, with optimal profile number selected via BLRT, BIC, theoretical support, and interpretability; BCH approach used to compare PISA scores across profiles while retaining classification uncertainty; pairwise profile comparisons used a Bonferroni-adjusted significance threshold (p<.0167).
column20: Three-step analysis: (1) CFA/MGCFA to establish cross-national measurement invariance of the four-factor social-emotional model; (2) country- specific LPA to identify latent social-emotional profiles; (3) BCH-based comparison of reading, math, and CPS scores across profiles within each country.
column21: Full measurement invariance was supported across all four countries. Three profiles emerged per country: Canada, USA, and Singapore showed "Sociable," "Reserved," and "Withdrawn" profiles, while China showed distinct "Team-oriented," "Reserved," and "Solitary" profiles. In Canada, USA, and Singapore, Sociable outperformed Reserved, which outperformed Withdrawn, on reading and math; a similar CPS pattern held in Canada/USA, but not in Singapore. In China, Team-oriented outperformed Reserved on all domains, but Solitary (low relationship skills) unexpectedly outperformed both Team-oriented (reading) and Reserved.
column22: The four-factor social-emotional model is cross-nationally comparable, but the profiles and their link to achievement differ between Western and Chinese contexts, aligning with cultural learning expectations. Strong relationship skills consistently benefited Western and Singaporean students, while in China, low-relationship students performed comparably or betterl. Findings caution against assuming one "adaptive" profile applies across cultures and call for culturally responsive SEL curricula.
column23: Only a small portion of each competency could be captured using existing PISA items, and one CASEL competency wasn't measured at all; findings from only four countries may not generalize; country is an imperfect proxy for culture, and no direct cultural-beliefs measure was included.
column24: Develop a dedicated social-emotional competencies scale (all five CASEL competencies) for future PISA cycles; extend comparisons to more countries; include direct measures of cultural beliefs to separate cultural from national effects.
column25: One of the first studies combining latent profile analysis with cross-national measurement invariance testing for social-emotional skills using PISA data; grounded in CASEL's SEL framework and cultural psychology theory.

column2: Ulas Ustun, Mustafa Cansiz, Ertugrul Ozdemir, and Nurcan Cansiz
column4: Student and School-Level Factors to Predict Science Literacy for Two Top-Performing Countries in PISA 2015: Finland and Singapore
column8: Science literacy; PISA; Finland; Singapore
column11: Student-level science literacy scores (plausible values) and predictor indices (affective, motivational, learning-time variables), plus school-level indices (ESCS, size, teacher qualifications) for Finland and Singapore.
column12: 5,882 students in Finland and 6,115 students in Singapore
column13: Hierarchical Linear Modeling (HLM), null models (ICC calculation), random-coefficients models (student-level), and means-as-outcomes models (school-level), with stepwise model comparison (chi-square/ deviance tests) to build parsimonious models
column15: Science literacy (10 plausible values)
column16: Student-level: test anxiety, expected occupational status, value cooperation, environmental optimism, epistemological beliefs, ESCS, interest in broad science topics, enjoyment of science , learning time (test language and science, LMINS/SMINS), out-of-school study time, teacher fairness, grade repetition. School-level: proportion of teachers with ISCED Level 6/PhD, school ESCS, school size
column17: To build separate hierarchical linear models identifying which student- and school-level factors predict science literacy in Finland and Singapore, two top-performing but educationally/ culturally distinct PISA 2015 countries, and compare the resulting models
column18:
1. Which student and school-level variables are significantly associated with students' science literacy in Finland and Singapore? 
2. How well do the hierarchical models predict science literacy in Finland and Singapore?
column19: Two-stage stratified random PISA sampling used per country; 10 plausible values used for science literacy per OECD guidance; stepwise model-building retained predictors only if statistically significant, explaining significant variance, and improving model fit (deviance/chi-square test); separate null, random-coefficients (student-level), and means-as-outcomes (school-level) models built per country.
column20: Three-stage HLM per country: (1) null model to compute ICC/variance decomposition; (2) random- coefficients model adding student-level predictors stepwise; (3) means-as-outcomes model adding school-level predictors stepwise; variance explained (effect size) calculated for each model.
column21: ICC was much smaller for Finland (0.13) than Singapore (0.38), indicating far more between-school variance in Singapore. Student-level models (8 predictors for Finland, 9 for Singapore) explained 43% (Finland) and 40% (Singapore) of within-school variance; top predictors were interest in broad science topics (Finland) and enjoyment of science (Singapore). Four predictors were shared across both countries in the same direction: epistemological beliefs, science learning time, and ESCS (all positive), and value cooperation. School-level models explained 61.5% (Finland) and 63.7% (Singapore) of between-school variance; school ESCS was by far the strongest predictor in both countries.
column22: Despite Finland and Singapore's very different educational and cultural systems (autonomy/ self-learning vs. competitive/ exam-driven), both share key predictors: affective factors (interest, enjoyment), epistemological beliefs, in-school science learning time, and especially ESCS at both student and school levels. This suggests no single "recipe" for educational success exists, but common underlying levers (fostering interest in science, addressing ESCS-related achievement gaps, and investing in teacher quality) may be broadly transferable across different educational contexts, even if not directly "copy-and-pasted".
column23: Cross-sectional PISA data precludes causal inference; several variables are self-reported and may be affected by cultural differences in response style, complicating direct cross- country descriptive comparisons; differing grade-level distributions between the two samples (mostly 9th grade in Finland vs. mostly 10th grade in Singapore) limit direct comparability.
column24: Not explicitly detailed as a standalone section beyond limitations; the paper implicitly calls for further investigation into causal relationships behind the identified associations, and into what drives between-school differences in Singapore specifically.
column25: Distinctive for its direct, parallel HLM comparison of two structurally very different but equally top-performing PISA countries (Finland: low-stakes, autonomy-oriented; Singapore: high-stakes, competitive); grounded in the multilevel "supply-use" model of student learning (Brühwiler & Blatchford, 2011), framing school/ teacher characteristics as "supply" that students "use" as learning opportunities.

column2: Fernando Martínez-Abad, Adriana Gamazo, and María-José Rodríguez-Conde
column4: Educational Data Mining: Identification of Factors Associated With School Effectiveness in PISA Assessment
column6: Web of Science and Google Scholar
column8: School effectiveness; large-scale assessments; educational data mining; academic achievement; hierarchical linear modeling
column11: School- and student-level data from the Spanish PISA 2015 sample, including performance tests in reading, mathematics, and science, along with context questionnaires administered to principals, teachers, and students, covering input and process variables.
column13: Hierarchical Linear Modeling to identify high/low-effectiveness schools via residuals; Decision trees (C4.5/J48) with 10-fold cross-validation
column15: Phase 1: student performance in mathematics, reading, and science. Phase 2: school effectiveness classification
column16: Phase 1 (input variables): school size, classroom size, resource/staff shortages, school ownership, student/teacher ratio, average ESCS, repeater rate, immigrant rate, proportion of girls. Phase 2 (process variables): 59 school- and aggregated student-level variables
column17: To propose a two-phase methodology combining multilevel modeling and decision trees to identify process factors associated with school effectiveness using PISA 2015.
column18:
1. Identify high- and low-effectiveness schools using multilevel models based on input variables.
2. Identify process factors most predictive of school effectiveness using decision trees, and evaluate the suitability of DTs for large-scale assessment data.
column19: Multilevel models run with 10 pVs and sample weights, robust estimators, missing data handled via low-percentage exclusion and regression imputation; schools classified as high-effectiveness or low- effectiveness; decision tree phase used student-level variables aggregated to school level, weighted by sample weights, tree size capped at 30 branches/minimum 15 instances per node, validated via 10-fold stratified cross-validation and tested for stability across 10 sub-samples.
column20: Phase 1: Multilevel (hierarchical linear) modeling to calculate school residuals and classify schools by effectiveness. Phase 2: C4.5/J48 decision tree classification using process variables as predictors and effectiveness classification as the target, evaluated via training-set fit and cross-validation (TP rate, precision, ROC-AUC, kappa, RRSE).
column21: ICC exceeded 10% in all 3 models, confirming sufficient school-level variance. The decision tree (25 branches, 13 leaves, 11 predictors) showed high fit (training ~92.5% accuracy; cross-validation 87.5%), outperforming prior EDM studies. Low effectiveness was linked to excessive extracurricular lessons, excessive ICT use, non-optimal reading time, excessive principal autonomy, and extreme student attitudes. High-effectiveness schools showed moderate, non-extreme values overall.
column22: The two-phase methodology outperformed prior EDM studies and avoided bias from using gross performance as the outcome. Findings align with prior literature but offer more precise thresholds; supports an inverse relationship between principal autonomy and effectiveness. Confirms decision trees as a useful complement to multilevel modeling.
column23: Cross-sectional design precludes causal inference; inconsistency across PISA cycles limits replicability; Spanish-only sample limits generalizability; outlier selection excluded 70% of the sample; aggregated student data at school level raises interpretive concerns.
column24: Replicate in other regions; conduct longitudinal studies; explore other techniques.
column25: Proposes a novel two-phase method (multilevel modeling + decision trees) within the Effective Schools Movement tradition, using the CIPO framework; implications for policy at macro, meso, and micro levels.

column2: Yimeng Liu and Jian Wang
column4: The Mediating–Moderating Model of Inquiry-Based Learning and Science Self-Efficacy: Evidence From PISA 2015
column8: Inquiry-based learning; science self-efficacy; science interest
column9: 57 PISA countries (35 OECD countries and 22 partner countries)
column11: Student-level WLE (weighted likelihood estimate) scores for inquiry-based teaching/ learning, science interest, science self-efficacy, teacher support, disciplinary climate, and gender.
column13: Mediation analysis (PROCESS Macro Model 4) and moderated mediation analysis (PROCESS Macro Model 59), both using 5,000 bootstrap samples with bias-corrected 95% confidence intervals
column15: Science self-efficacy (SCIEEFF, WLE score)
column16: Inquiry-based science teaching/learning practices; mediator: interest in broad science topics; moderator: teacher support in science classes; controls: gender, disciplinary climate in science classes
column17: To clarify the mechanism by which inquiry-based learning influences science self-efficacy, testing a mediating-moderating model in which science interest mediates the relationship and teacher support moderates both the direct and indirect effects.
column18:
1. How is science interest associated with the relationship between inquiry-based learning and science self-efficacy? 
2. How is this association moderated by teacher support?
column19: PISA 2015 categorical questionnaire items scaled via IRT and converted to WLE scores (M=0, SD=1 across 35 OECD countries); only the 57 countries with complete data on all variables of interest included; all focal variables standardized (4-point Likert-based WLE scores).
column20: Mediation analysis (PROCESS Model 4) testing whether science interest mediates the inquiry- based learning, science self-efficacy relationship, decomposing total/direct/indirect effects; moderated mediation analysis (PROCESS Model 59) testing whether teacher support moderates both the direct path and the two legs of the indirect (mediated) path, controlling for gender and disciplinary climate.
column21: Inquiry-based learning was significantly positively correlated with science self-efficacy (total effect B=0.194, p<.001). Science interest partially mediated this relationship, with the indirect effect (B=0.039) accounting for 20.1% of the total effect and the direct effect (B=0.155) accounting for 79.9%. Teacher support significantly and positively moderated the direct effect of inquiry-based learning on self-efficacy, but significantly moderated the science-interest mediated indirect path negatively.
column22: The study clarifies "how" (via science interest) and "when" (depending on teacher support level) inquiry-based learning translates into science self-efficacy, contributing both theoretically and practically to the design of inquiry-based science instruction. The counterintuitive negative moderation of the indirect (interest-based) pathway by teacher support suggests high teacher support may substitute for or diminish the role of intrinsic interest in building self-efficacy, warranting further theoretical exploration.
column23: Finer-grained subgroup analyses and non-self-report methods are needed to understand classroom-level mechanisms; the model only examines student-level factors, omitting school- and country-level factors that multilevel/hierarchical modeling could capture; other potential moderators beyond science interest and teacher support were not examined; cross-sectional design precludes causal interpretation.
column24: Use multilevel/hierarchical linear modeling to incorporate school- and country-level factors; explore additional mediators, moderators, and control variables; employ non-self- report methods to study classroom- level teacher support and inquiry behaviors in more detail; conduct longitudinal and experimental studies to test causal and developmental dynamics in the inquiry-based learning–self-efficacy relationship.
column25: Grounded in Bandura's reciprocal determinism and self-efficacy theory; one of the larger-scale (57-country, 346,109-student) applications of a formal mediation-moderation (PROCESS macro) framework to PISA science education data, offering a nuanced account of how and under what conditions inquiry-based learning benefits students' science self-efficacy.

column2: Serap Büyükk?d?k
column4: Influential Factors on Mathematical Literacy of Turkish Students: An Educational Data Mining Study Using PISA 2015 Data
column8: Educational data mining; J48; Multilayer perceptron; Naïve Bayes; Support vector machine
column11: Student-level data on mathematics literacy (PVMATH) dichotomized as successful/unsuccessful, plus 13 predictor variables spanning demographics, motivation, and family background.
column12: 5,895 Turkish students from 61 provinces and 187 schools
column13: Multilayer Perceptron (MLP), J48 decision tree, Support Vector Machine (SVM), and Naïve Bayes classifiers; feature selection via InfoGain AttributeEval, GainRatio AttributeEval, and Chi- Squared AttributedEval; 10-fold cross-validation
column15: Mathematical literacy, dichotomized as successful/unsuccessful based on the PISA 2015 Turkey average score (cut-off = 420, derived from PVMATH)
column16: 13 variables retained after feature selection: grade level, gender, parental support, test anxiety, achievement motivation, enjoyment of cooperation, sense of belonging to school, learning time in mathematics, total weekly learning time, out-of-school study time in mathematics, mother's education, father's education, and highest parental education
column17: To classify Turkish students as successful/unsuccessful in PISA 2015 mathematical literacy using four data mining methods, identify the most important predictor variables, and compare classifier performance across multiple evaluation criteria.
column18:
1. Which variables related to mathematical literacy are important for classifying students? 
2. How are the descriptive statistics on the important variables for successful and unsuccessful students? 
3. Based on five evaluation criteria (F-measure, Precision, Recall, MCC, ROC), which data mining method (MLP, J48, SVM, Naïve Bayes) performs best in classifying students as successful/ unsuccessful in mathematical literacy?
column19: Missing data imputed prior to analysis; mathematics literacy converted from continuous (PVMATH) to categorical (success/failure) using the Turkey average (420) as cut-off; feature selection using three attribute-evaluation methods reduced initial variable pool to 13 significant predictors; reliability of PISA questionnaire scales confirmed (McDonald's ? all >0.70); ethics committee approval obtained.
column20: Four classification algorithms (MLP, J48, SVM, Naïve Bayes) trained and evaluated via 10-fold cross-validation on the reduced 13-variable feature set, compared using Precision, Recall, F-measure, Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC), and ROC.
column21: Total weekly learning time and father's education level were the most important variables for classifying successful vs. unsuccessful students. No single method outperformed all others across all criteria: SVM performed best on Recall/F-measure for the unsuccessful-student category; J48 performed best overall on F-measure, Recall, and MCC; Naïve Bayes had the highest ROC (0.720) and best Precision. MLP consistently performed worst across most criteria. Overall classification values ranged from 0.643 to 0.720, indicating acceptable but modest classification accuracy. Gender, grade level, and family background were all significantly associated with mathematical literacy.
column22: Family background (parental education) and learning time were confirmed as key drivers of mathematical literacy, consistent with broader PISA literature; gender differences persisted but were framed as likely socio-cultural rather than biological in origin, with implications for inclusive curriculum design. No single data mining method was universally superior, reinforcing the recommendation that researchers use at least two methods for more robust/accurate EDM results.

column15: Self-reported lesson-aim attainment (SLAA)  7-item teacher-reported measure of how far lessons taught in the previous week achieved specified instructional/classroom-management aims; primary outcome dichotomized as "relatively high"; continuous version and 70th/80th percentile thresholds used in sensitivity analyses
column16: Teacher background (gender, age group, employment/work-time status), education-system context (country/economy, ISCED level), and 20-item broad work-related stress index. AI-added block: perceived AI benefits, perceived AI risks, breadth of AI task use, AI-related barriers ("overwhelmed by integrating new technologies").
column17: To test, using a nested explainable machine-learning framework, whether AI-related measures (perceived benefits/ risks, breadth of task use, barriers) provide incremental predictive information for relatively high self- reported lesson-aim attainment, beyond teacher background, work- related stress, and education- system context, across 55 countries/ economies.
column18: Do AI-related measures provide incremental predictive information for relatively high self-reported lesson-aim attainment among teachers, beyond what is already explained by teacher background, work-related stress, and education-system context?
column19: Codebook-aware TALIS cleaning to avoid misinterpreting survey-specific response codes as substantive values; continuous SLAA score computed as the mean of >=4 valid items among 7; binary outcome defined relative to the 75th percentile within each country/economy × ISCED stratum; train-only imputation with missingness indicators; AI-module items with substantial routing-related missingness retained via missingness flags; matched nested LightGBM models trained/validated using country-by-school grouped splits with early stopping; SHAP values computed on a fixed random sample for the final AI-added model; robustness checks.
column20: A nested explainable machine-learning framework was developed using TALIS 2024 teacher data to test the incremental predictive information supplied by AI-related measures. The participants were 88,991 primary, lower-secondary, and upper- secondary teachers from 55 countries who were eligible for the AI-module analysis and had a valid outcome. The seven-item outcome captured teachers’ reports of how far lessons taught in the previous week achieved specified instructional and classroom management aims; a relatively high indicator denoted scores at or above the 75th percentile within the same country/economy and ISCED stratum. Matched baseline and AI-added regularized LightGBM models were compared using country-by-school grouped validation and early stopping. Threshold, continuous-outcome, survey-weighted-evaluation, missingness, and country-heterogeneity sensitivity analyses were conducted.
column21:
In the final matched analysis, the AI-added model increased independent-test AUROC from 0.6021 to 0.6299 and AUPRC from 0.4138 to 0.4476, while reducing the Brier score from 0.2114 to 0.2071 and log loss from 0.6126 to 0.6029. Paired bootstrap intervals indicated statistically stable, but practically modest, gains (observed AUROC=0.0277, 95% CI 0.0215–0.0334; observed AUPRC=0.0338, 95% CI 0.0262–0.0411). AUROC gains were similar
at the 70th and 80th percentile thresholds, and the continuous-outcome R^2 increased from 0.1745 to 0.1911. Country-specific AUROC gains were positive
in 48 of 55 countries/economies but varied substantially.
column22:
AI-related perceptions and breadth of task use supplied modest
incremental predictive information for predicting relatively high self-reported lesson aimattainment. “Relatively high”denotes only a within-country and ISCED ranking and does not indicate objectively superior teaching or better student learning. The modest discrimination, cross- sectional design, routed missingness, and self-reported outcome preclude causal interpretation and use for teacher screening or other high-stakes individual decisions. Public-health relevance is presented as a potential extension to future research in health-promoting school settings, not as a directly measured outcome.
column23: Cross-sectional design precludes establishing temporal ordering/causality; SLAA is a recent, class-specific teacher self-report, and its upper-quartile label is only a relative within-context ranking, not an objective/cross-national performance standard; substantial AI-module missingness may confound observed breadth with eligibility/questionnaire-pathway information, and train-only imputation does not correct for unmeasured selection bias; unweighted model fitting targets the analytic sample rather than design-based TALIS populations, and weighted results changed baseline performance and incremental magnitude meaningfully; the 20-item stress index's high reliability may partly reflect item count rather than a single coherent latent construct.
column24: Conduct longitudinal and intervention studies to test whether AI adoption precedes changes in independently assessed teaching practices; combine teacher reports with student health literacy, learning outcomes, classroom observations, or administrative indicators to reduce common-method bias; conduct dedicated, directly sampled studies in mental health education, nutrition education, disease-prevention education, or health-promotion programs to test whether similar predictive patterns hold.
column25: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to support teachers’ lesson planning, feedback, assessment, and learning-material adaptation in school settings. Effective teaching practices may also support health literacy, social-emotional development, and health-promoting learning environments, although TALIS does not directly measure public-health education outcomes. Existing studies often treat AI use as a simple adoption variable and provide limited cross-national evidence on whether AI-related measures provide incremental predictive information after accounting for teacher background, teachers’work-related stress, and education-system context.

column18:
1. How widely is access to professional learning for teacher AI literacy distributed across participating education systems? 
2. To what extent is teachers' declared need for AI-related professional learning associated with the probability of having participated in such learning? 
3. Do teachers' prior digital and professional capital predict access beyond declared need? 
4. Which school-level digital and organisational conditions are associated with higher probability of access?
5. Does the association between declared need and access vary across education systems?
column19: Analytic sample restricted to teachers with valid data on AI-related professional learning participation and declared need (administered only in relevant teacher questionnaire forms); sequential sample construction documented transparently (Table 1); common analytic sample (108,136 teachers, 10,840 schools) used consistently across nested model comparisons to avoid confounding sample composition changes with model changes; teacher sampling weights and school- clustering incorporated throughout.
column20: Sequential empirical strategy: (1) weighted prevalence estimation of AI-related professional learning participation per education system; (2) descriptive/Rao-Scott test of the declared need participation association; (3) three-level null model for variance decomposition (teacher/school/ system); (4) sequential three-level linear probability models adding declared need, then teacher-level digital/professional capital, then school-level digital/organisational conditions; (5) random-slope models testing whether the need access association varies across education systems.
column21: Participation ranged from <10% (France) to >75% (Singapore) across systems. Most variance was at the teacher level (81.8%), with 9.7% at school level and 8.5% at system level. Declared need showed a non-monotonic relationship with participation: low and moderate need predicted higher participation (+7.7 and +10.7 points), but high need showed no significant advantage. Digital self-efficacy and professional collaboration were consistently linked to higher participation. School-level digital resources and leadership support also mattered. The need-participation link varied significantly across education systems.
column22: Access to AI-related professional learning is patterned by existing digital confidence, collaboration, and school capacity rather than driven by need. Teachers with the greatest need are not reached more than moderate-need teachers, suggesting equitable teacher AI literacy requires deliberate opportunity structures, not just competence frameworks or voluntary participation.
column23: TALIS 2024 measures only participation in professional learning, not actual AI literacy, competence, or classroom use; cross-sectional design precludes causal inference; measures are self-reported; system-level policy mechanisms weren't directly measured, so cross-system differences remain hypothesis-generating.
column24: Longitudinal studies on whether access leads to later literacy/ classroom gains; qualitative research on why some systems convert need into access better than others; studies on the quality and equity effects of professional learning, not just participation.
column25: Uses TALIS 2024's new AI-related professional learning items; frames its contribution as evidence of unequal access to a learning opportunity, not evidence of achieved AI literacy.

column17: To determine the most important socio-economic/demographic variables affecting mathematics achievement of 15-year-olds in 12 Asia-Pacific PISA 2018 countries using educational data mining (classification + feature importance), and to explore whether countries cluster similarly based on these educational predictors versus their broader socio-economic development levels.
column18:
1. Identify high-importance variables affecting mathematics achievement across the 12 Asia-Pacific countries via classification models and feature importance.
2. Cluster the countries based on both feature-importance profiles and socio-economic indicators to examine whether educational attainment and socio-economic development are related.
column19: 5 of 10 plausible values randomly selected per student, each dichotomized against the OECD math average (489); class imbalance addressed via down-sampling (majority class down-sampled to match minority); % of raw data dropped during preprocessing (final N=86,886 combined across countries); grid search used for LR/RF/SVM hyperparameter tuning; PFI computed using best-parameter models; analyses repeated separately across 5 sampled PVs.
column20: Country-specific classification models (LR, RF, SVM) trained to classify math achievement, compared via accuracy/precision/recall/F1 averaged across sampled PVs; PFI applied to identify top predictive features per country; two separate hierarchical clustering analyses conducted visualized via dendrograms and compared via a tanglegram; robustness check comparing model performance using all features vs. only high-importance features.
column21: SVM had the best overall accuracy, slightly ahead of LR and RF; the best algorithm varied by country. Common top predictors across all 12 countries: parental education, access to educational resources, age, weekly lesson time, and age of starting kindergarten; books at home and weekly science/ language class hours were also consistently important. Restricting models to high-importance features only slightly reduced accuracy for RF and LR, more so for SVM. Clustering grouped Korea, Japan, and Taipei together, and separately grouped Thailand, China, Indonesia, and Malaysia together in both analyses.
column22: High-importance features drive most of the classification performance, though lower- importance features still contribute. Findings on class-time and kindergarten attendance align with prior literature; "books at home" was the strongest home-resource predictor across all countries. The convergence between the two clustering analyses supports a link between countries' educational attainment patterns and socio-economic development.
column23: Not explicitly detailed as a standalone limitations section in the extracted text.
column24: Extend the analysis to include PISA science literacy and reading proficiency results at a larger scale; apply the same EDM methodology developed here to other national/international large-scale assessments.
column25: Distinctive for combining a 3-algorithm classification/feature-importance approach with a dual clustering design to explicitly test the education socioeconomic development relationship across a within-region (Asia-Pacific) comparative sample, rather than a single-country PISA analysis.

column4: Optimizing automated scoring in ILSAs with prompt compression

column16: Prompt configuration: (1) Baseline (original passage + original SG); (2) Model 1 (original passage + RefinedSG_ET); (3) Model 2 (summarized passage + RefinedSG_ET); (4) Model 3 (summarized passage + RefinedSG_AT)
column17: To evaluate whether prompt compression of reading passages and scoring guides can maintain automated scoring accuracy while improving efficiency and reducing cost in multilingual ILSAs.
column18:
1. To what extent does prompt compression reduce token length for reading passages and scoring guides? 
2. Does compression maintain automated scoring accuracy and kappa comparable to the baseline? 
3. Does compression affect hallucination rates? 
4. What are the cost and time implications of compression-based AS?
column19: 20% random subset selected per country; responses processed through GPT-4o pipeline; passages summarized per item using Zero-Shot-CoT; SGs refined via extractive (Python parsing) or abstractive (GPT-4o) methods; JSON output format enforced; post-processing: misformatted outputs corrected via Python; hallucinations detected via translation-length ratio (threshold 2.2× for Latin-alphabet, 20× for non-Latin) and reassigned score 0.
column20: Stepwise model comparison (Baseline, Model 1, Model 2, Model 3); each model differs in passage and SG treatment; evaluated on compression ratio, accuracy, ?, hallucination rate, running time, and cost; in-depth analysis of Model 3 via confusion matrices to identify misalignment sources (human scoring inconsistency vs. AS error).
column21: Model 3 compressed passages to ~18% and scoring guides to ~15% of their original length. Despite this, accuracy remained high (92.87% vs. 92.62% baseline) and kappa was nearly equivalent (0.80 vs. 0.82). Cost dropped by 76% (~$3.62 vs. ~$15–17 per item). Hallucination rate stayed low (0.12% vs. 0.05%). Misalignment came mainly from two sources: human raters scoring similar responses inconsistently (Items 1, 2, 5), and GPT-4o struggling with nuanced or low-resource language responses (Items 3, 4).
column22: Prompt compression is viable for AS in multilingual reading assessments. RefinedSG_AT outperforms ET by achieving greater compression (R=0.15 vs. 0.25) with equal or better accuracy. Query-based summarization retains question-relevant content effectively. CoT and meta-prompting improve consistency and minimize hallucinations across 29 languages. Compressed AS offers a scalable, cost-effective alternative to human scoring in ILSAs.
column23: Only 20% of the full dataset analyzed; limited to 5 secured items (unpublishable); hallucination detection relies on heuristic length ratios; misalignment source identification is qualitative, not automated; study does not assess fairness or systematic bias across languages/countries.
column24: Validate on full PIRLS dataset and additional CR items; automate misalignment source detection using semantic clustering; use ensemble of LLMs (e.g., Llama, Claude) as third-party evaluators; examine fairness and systematic bias across languages before operational use.
column25: Items are secured for PIRLS 2026 reuse, not published. Enterprise-level API used (GDPR-compliant, no training data usage). Builds on Jung et al. (2022, 2024, 2025) series on AS in ILSAs. First study to apply prompt compression specifically to reading assessment AS in an ILSA context. GPT-4o temperature set to 0 for determinism

column8: PISA 2022; clustering analysis; machine learning; regression models; PCA; educational achievement; education policies
column11: Country-level dataset with one observation per country, containing average Mathematics, Reading, Science, and overall PISA scores (no individual student data used).
column13: Pearson correlation analysis; PCA; regression models (classical Linear Regression, Ridge Regression, Huber Regressor); unsupervised clustering (K-Means, Hierarchical, Gaussian Mixture Model, DBSCAN); t-SNE for 3D visualization; supervised classification models (RF, Extra Trees, Support Vector Classifier, Multilayer Perceptron) embedded in stratified k-fold cross-validation
